**Granada** ([/ɡ r ə ˈ n ɑː d ə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_grə-NAH-də_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-8)Spanish:[[ɡɾaˈnaða]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/d/da/Pronunciation_of_Granada_in_Spanish.ogg/Pronunciation_of_Granada_in_Spanish.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pronunciation_of_Granada_in_Spanish.ogg "File:Pronunciation of Granada in Spanish.ogg")) is the [capital city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city "Capital city") of the [province of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Granada "Province of Granada"), in the [autonomous community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_communities_of_Spain "Autonomous communities of Spain") of [Andalusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusia "Andalusia"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"). Granada is located at the foot of the [Sierra Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Nevada_(Spain) "Sierra Nevada (Spain)") mountains, at the confluence of four rivers, the [Darro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darro_(river) "Darro (river)"), the [Genil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genil "Genil"), the [Monachil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monachil_(river) "Monachil (river)") and the Beiro. Ascribed to the [Vega de Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vega_de_Granada "Vega de Granada")_comarca_, the city sits at an average elevation of 738 m (2,421 ft)[above sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Above_mean_sea_level "Above mean sea level") 50 km from the [Mediterranean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean "Mediterranean") coast, the [Costa Tropical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Tropical "Costa Tropical"). With a population of 233,532 as of 2024, it is the [20th-largest city in Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_of_Spain#By_population "List of municipalities of Spain") and is an important [wine growing region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_(wine) "Granada (wine)") It was the last Muslim stronghold in Islamic Spain.

Nearby is the [Sierra Nevada Ski Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Nevada_Ski_Station "Sierra Nevada Ski Station"), where the [FIS Alpine World Ski Championships 1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIS_Alpine_World_Ski_Championships_1996 "FIS Alpine World Ski Championships 1996") were held. Its nearest airport is [Federico García Lorca Granada-Jaén Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Garc%C3%ADa_Lorca_Airport "Federico García Lorca Airport").

The area was settled since ancient times by [Iberians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberians "Iberians"), [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome"), and [Visigoths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visigothic_Kingdom "Visigothic Kingdom"). The current settlement became a major city of [Al-Andalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Andalus "Al-Andalus") in the 11th century during the [Zirid Taifa of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa_of_Granada "Taifa of Granada").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9) In the 13th century it became the capital of the [Emirate of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Granada "Emirate of Granada") under [Nasrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasrid_dynasty "Nasrid dynasty") rule, the last [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam")-ruled state in the [Iberian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula"). Granada was [conquered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_War "Granada War") in 1492 by the [Catholic Monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Monarchs_of_Spain "Catholic Monarchs of Spain") and progressively transformed into a [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians "Christians") city over the course of the 16th century.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColeman2013-10)

The [Alhambra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra "Alhambra"), a medieval Nasrid citadel and palace, is located in Granada. It is one of the most famous monuments of [Islamic architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_architecture "Islamic architecture")[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBloom2020151-11) and one of the most visited tourist sites in Spain.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-13) Islamic-period influence and [Moorish architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorish_architecture "Moorish architecture") are also preserved in the [Albaicín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albaic%C3%ADn "Albaicín") neighborhood and other medieval monuments in the city.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:24-14) The 16th century also saw a flourishing of [Mudéjar architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar_art "Mudéjar art") and [Renaissance architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_architecture "Renaissance architecture"),[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColeman201370,_89-15) followed later by [Baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque_architecture "Baroque architecture") and [Churrigueresque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Churrigueresque "Churrigueresque") styles.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-17) The [University of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Granada "University of Granada") has an estimated 47,000 undergraduate students spread over five different campuses in the city. The [pomegranate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomegranate "Pomegranate") ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _granada_) is the [heraldic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heraldry "Heraldry") device of Granada.

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

Granada's historical name in the [Arabic language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language") was غرناطة (_\_Ġarnāṭa\__).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERingSalkinLa_Boda1995296-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoom2006149-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDale1882-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEl_Hareir2011454-21) Both the name's meaning and origin are uncertain and have been debated.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:5-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:13-23) The toponym definitely existed prior to the [Zirid period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa_of_Granada "Taifa of Granada") in the 11th century.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:13-23) It probably first appeared in the 9th century[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:5-22) and it is found in Arabic sources from the 10th century.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEViguera-Mol%C3%ADns202120-24)

The word _Gárnata_ (or _Karnata_) possibly meant "hill of strangers".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-25):41[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-26) Another meaning might be "hill of pilgrims".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:5-22) It could even have been of [Berber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berber_languages "Berber languages") origin.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEViguera-Mol%C3%ADns202120-24) Another theory is that it derived from [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin")_granum_ (or its plural _grana_), meaning "seed", "beads", or a "scarlet colour", which would have been adapted into Arabic as _\_Ġarnāṭa\__ or _\_Iġranāṭa\__.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEViguera-Mol%C3%ADns202120-24) The Arab chronicler [Al-Maqqari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Maqqari "Al-Maqqari") believed that it came from the Latin word for [pomegranate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomegranate "Pomegranate"), _granata_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:5-22) In either case, the Latin word may have been used not in its primary sense, but in the more derived sense of "red", referring to the colour of the area's soil and its buildings. This would also mirror the etymology of the name of the [Alhambra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra "Alhambra").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:13-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEViguera-Mol%C3%ADns202120-24)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

See also: [Granada chronology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_chronology "Granada chronology")

### Pre-Umayyad history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Pre-Umayyad history")]

See also: [Hispania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispania "Hispania")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Arqueol%C3%B3gico_03_%2842189174461%29.jpg/250px-Arqueol%C3%B3gico_03_%2842189174461%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arqueol%C3%B3gico_03_(42189174461).jpg)

[Mosaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_mosaic "Roman mosaic") from a [Roman villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_villa "Roman villa"), dating from 1 AD, discovered in the district of Los Mondragones in Granada (now kept at the [Archaeological Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeological_Museum_of_Granada "Archaeological Museum of Granada"))[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:5-22)

The region surrounding what today is Granada has been populated since at least 5500 BC.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERingSalkinLa_Boda1995296-18) Archeological artifacts found in the city indicate that the site of the city, including the area around the present-day avenue of _Gran Vía de Colón_, was inhabited since the [Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age"). The most ancient ruins found in the area belong to an [oppidum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oppidum "Oppidum") called _Ilturir_, founded by the [Iberian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberians "Iberians")[Bastetani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastetani "Bastetani") tribe around 650 BC.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:5-22) The name Elibyrge is also attested in reference to this area.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERingSalkinLa_Boda1995296-18) This settlement became later known as _Iliberri_ or _Iliberis_.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERingSalkinLa_Boda1995296-18)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodgersCavendish20216%E2%80%9310-27)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:5-22) In 44 BC _Iliberis_ became a [Roman colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonia_(Roman) "Colonia (Roman)") and in 27 BC it became a Roman _[municipium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipium "Municipium")_ named _Florentia Iliberritana_ ('Flourishing Iliberri').[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:5-22)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodgersCavendish20216%E2%80%9310-27)

The identification of present-day Granada with the Roman-era _Iliberis_ and the historical continuity between the two settlements has long been debated by scholars.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:0522-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:2-29)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodgersCavendish20216%E2%80%9310-27) Modern archeological digs on the [Albaicín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albaic%C3%ADn "Albaicín") hill have uncovered finds demonstrating the presence of a significant Roman town on that site.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodgersCavendish20216%E2%80%9310-27) Little is known, however, about the history of the city in the period between the end of the [Roman era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispania "Hispania") and the 11th century.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodgersCavendish20216%E2%80%9310-27) An important Christian [synod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synod "Synod") circa 300 AD, the [Synod of Elvira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synod_of_Elvira "Synod of Elvira"), took place near this area (the name _Elvira_ being derived from the name _Iliberri_), but there is no concrete archeological or documentary evidence establishing the exact location of the meeting. It may have taken place in the former Roman town or it may have taken place somewhere in the surrounding region, which was known as Elvira.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodgersCavendish20216%E2%80%9310-27)

### Founding and early history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Founding and early history")]

The [Umayyad conquest of Hispania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_conquest_of_Hispania "Umayyad conquest of Hispania"), starting in 711 AD, brought large parts of the Iberian Peninsula under Moorish control and established [al-Andalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Andalus "Al-Andalus"). The earliest Arabic historical sources mention that a town named _Qashtīliya_, later known as _[Madīnat Ilbīra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madinat\_Ilbira "Madinat Ilbira")_ (Elvira), was located on the southern slopes of the Sierra de Elvira mountains (near present-day [Atarfe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atarfe "Atarfe")) and became the most important settlement in the area.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:2-29)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodgersCavendish20216%E2%80%9310-27) A smaller settlement and fortress (_ḥiṣn_) named _Ġarnāṭa_ (also transliterated as _Gharnāṭa)_ existed on the south side of the Darro River or on the site of the current Albaicín neighbourhood. The latter had a mainly [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews") population and thus was also known as _Gharnāṭat al-Yahūd_ ("_Gharnāṭa_ of the Jews").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodgersCavendish20216%E2%80%9310-27) The district around the city was known as _[Kūrat Ilbīra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kura\_(al-Andalus)#K%C5%ABra\_of\_Elvira "Kura (al-Andalus)")_ (roughly "Province of Elvira"). After 743 the town of _Ilbīra_ was settled by soldiers from the region of [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria_(region) "Syria (region)") who played a role in supporting [Abd al-Rahman I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Rahman_I "Abd al-Rahman I"), the founder of the [Emirate of Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Emirate of Córdoba") and a new [Umayyad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_dynasty "Umayyad dynasty") dynasty.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9) In the late 9th century, during the reign of [Abdallah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdullah_ibn_Muhammad_al-Umawi "Abdullah ibn Muhammad al-Umawi") (r. 844–912), the city and its surrounding district were the site of conflict between _[muwallads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muwallad "Muwallad")_ (Muslim converts) who were loyal to the central government and Arabs, led by Sawwār ibn Ḥamdūn, who resented them.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-30)

At the beginning of the 11th century, the area became dominated by the Zirids, a [Sanhaja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanhaja "Sanhaja")[Berber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berbers "Berbers") group and offshoot of the [Zirids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zirid_dynasty "Zirid dynasty") who ruled parts of [North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Africa "North Africa"). This group became an important contingent in the army of [ʿAbd al-Malik al-Muẓaffar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Malik_al-Muzaffar "Abd al-Malik al-Muzaffar"), the prime minister of Caliph [Hisham II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hisham_II "Hisham II") (r. 976–1009) and successor to [Ibn Abi ʿAmir al-Mansur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almanzor "Almanzor") (Almanzor) as _de facto_ ruler of the [Caliphate of Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Caliphate of Córdoba"). For their service, the Zirids were granted control of the province of Elvira.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9) When the Caliphate collapsed after 1009 and the [Fitna (civil war)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitna_of_al-Andalus "Fitna of al-Andalus") began, the Zirid leader [Zawi ben Ziri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zawi_ben_Ziri "Zawi ben Ziri") established an independent kingdom for himself, the [Taifa of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa_of_Granada "Taifa of Granada"). Arab sources such as [al-Idrisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_al-Idrisi "Muhammad al-Idrisi") consider him to be the founder of the city of Granada.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9) His [great-grandnephew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdallah_ibn_Buluggin "Abdallah ibn Buluggin")'s surviving "memoirs," known as the _Tibyan_ – the only ones for the Spanish "Middle Ages" – provide considerable detail for this brief period.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:3-31) Because _Madīnat Ilbīra_ was situated on a low plain and, as a result, difficult to protect from attacks, the ruler decided to transfer his residence to the higher situated area of _Ġarnāṭa_. According to Arabic sources _Ilbīra_ was razed during the Fitna, afterwards it was not restored at its previous place and instead _Ġarnāṭa_, the former Jewish town, replaced it as the main city. In a short time this town was transformed into one of the most important cities of [al-Andalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Andalus "Al-Andalus").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERingSalkinLa_Boda1995296-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDale1882-20) Until the 11th century it had a mixed population of Christians, Muslims, and Jews.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:24-14)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/PuertaMonaita.JPG/250px-PuertaMonaita.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PuertaMonaita.JPG)

Puerta Monaita, one of the 11th-century Zirid gates in the [Albaicin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albaic%C3%ADn "Albaicín")

The Zirids built their citadel and palace, known as the _al-Qaṣaba al-Qadīma_ ("Old Citadel"), on the hill now occupied by the Albaicín neighborhood.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:24-14) It was connected to two smaller fortresses on the Sabika hill (site of the future Alhambra) and Mauror hill to the south.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:24-14) The city around it grew during the 11th century to include the Albaicín, the Sabika, the Mauror, and a part of the surrounding plains. The city was fortified with walls encompassing an area of approximately 75 [hectares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hectare "Hectare").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9) The northern part of these walls, near the Albaicin citadel, have survived to the present day, along with two of its gates: _Bāb al-Unaydar_ (now called _Puerta Monaita_ in Spanish) and _Bāb al-Ziyāda_ (now known as _Arco de las Pesas_ or _Puerta Nueva_).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:24-14)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9) The city and its residences were supplied with water through an extensive network of underground [cisterns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cistern "Cistern") and pipes.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:052232-32) On the Darro River, along the wall connecting the Zirid citadel with the Sabika hill, was a [sluice gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sluice_gate "Sluice gate") called _Bāb al-Difāf_ ("Gate of the Tambourines"), which could be closed or opened to control the flow of the river and retain water if necessary.[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-34)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTER%C4%97klaityt%C4%972021443%E2%80%93445-33)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodgersCavendish202121-35) The nearby [Bañuelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Ba%C3%B1uelo "El Bañuelo"), a former [hammam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammam "Hammam") (bathhouse), also likely dates from this time, as does the former [minaret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minaret "Minaret") of a [mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque") in the Albaicín, now part of the Church of San José.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:24-14)

Under the Zirid kings [Habbus ibn Maksan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habbus_al-Muzaffar "Habbus al-Muzaffar") and [Badis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badis_ibn_Habus "Badis ibn Habus"), the most powerful figure was the Jewish administrator known as [Samuel ha-Nagid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_ibn_Naghrillah "Samuel ibn Naghrillah") (in [Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language")) or Isma'il ibn Nagrilla (in Arabic). Samuel was a highly educated member of the former elites of Cordoba, who fled that city after the outbreak of the Fitna. He eventually found his way to Granada, where Habbus ibn Maksan appointed him his secretary in 1020 and entrusted him with many important responsibilities, including tax collection. Under Badis, he even took charge of the army.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:4-36) During this period, the Muslim king was looked upon as a mainly symbolic figurehead. Granada was the centre of Jewish Sephardi culture and scholarship. According to Daniel Eisenberg:

> Granada was in the eleventh century the center of Sephardic civilization at its peak, and from 1027 until 1066 Granada was a powerful Jewish state. Jews did not hold the foreigner ([dhimmi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhimmi "Dhimmi")) status typical of Islamic rule. Samuel ibn Nagrilla, recognized by Sephardic Jews everywhere as the quasi-political ha-Nagid ('The Prince'), was king in all but name. As vizier he made policy and—much more unusual—led the army. [...] It is said that Samuel's strengthening and fortification of Granada was what permitted it, later, to survive as the last Islamic state in the Iberian peninsula. All of the greatest figures of eleventh-century Hispano-Jewish culture are associated with Granada. [Moses Ibn Ezra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Ibn_Ezra "Moses Ibn Ezra") was from Granada; on his invitation [Judah ha-Levi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judah_ha-Levi "Judah ha-Levi") spent several years there as his guest. [Ibn Gabirol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Gabirol "Ibn Gabirol")’s patrons and hosts were the Jewish [viziers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vizier "Vizier") of Granada, Samuel ha-Nagid and his son Joseph.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-37)

After Samuel's death, his son Joseph took over after his position but proved to lack his father's diplomacy, bringing on the [1066 Granada massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1066_Granada_massacre "1066 Granada massacre"),[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:4-36) which ended the [Golden age of Jewish culture in Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_age_of_Jewish_culture_in_Spain "Golden age of Jewish culture in Spain").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

From the late 11th century to the early 13th century, Al-Andalus was dominated by two successive North African Berber empires. The [Almoravids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almoravids "Almoravids") ruled Granada from 1090 and the [Almohads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_dynasty "Almohad dynasty") from 1166.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHourihane2012-38) Granada also served as an administrative capital of Almoravid rule in al-Andalus.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKennedy1996172-39) Evidence from the artistic and archeological remains of this period suggest that the city thrived under the Almoravids but declined under the Almohads.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:24-14) Remnants of the Almohad period in the city include the [Alcázar Genil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_Genil "Alcázar Genil"), built in 1218–1219 (but later redecorated under the Nasrids),[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEArnold2017240%E2%80%93241-40) and possibly the former minaret attached to the present-day Church of San Juan de los Reyes in the Albaicin.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-41)[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-43)

### Nasrid Emirate of Granada

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Nasrid Emirate of Granada")]

Main article: [Emirate of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Granada "Emirate of Granada")

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/CoA_Nasrid_kings_Alhambra_Granada_Spain.jpg/250px-CoA_Nasrid_kings_Alhambra_Granada_Spain.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CoA_Nasrid_kings_Alhambra_Granada_Spain.jpg)

Sigil of the [Nasrid dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasrid_dynasty "Nasrid dynasty") located in the Palacio de Comares

In 1228 [Idris al-Ma'mun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idris_al-Ma'mun "Idris al-Ma'mun"), the last effective [Almohad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_Caliphate "Almohad Caliphate") ruler in al-Andalus, left the Iberian Peninsula. As Almohad rule collapsed local leaders and factions emerged across the region. With the _[Reconquista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista "Reconquista")_ in full swing, the Christian kingdoms of [Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Castile "Kingdom of Castile") and [Aragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aragon "Kingdom of Aragon") – under kings [Ferdinand III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_III_of_Castile "Ferdinand III of Castile") and [James I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_I_of_Aragon "James I of Aragon"), respectively – made major conquests across al-Andalus. Castile captured [Cordoba in 1236](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_C%C3%B3rdoba_(1236) "Siege of Córdoba (1236)") and [Seville in 1248](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Seville "Siege of Seville"). Meanwhile, the ambitious [Ibn al-Ahmar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_I_of_Granada "Muhammad I of Granada") (Muhammad I) established what became the last and longest reigning [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim") dynasty in the Iberian peninsula, the [Nasrids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasrid_dynasty "Nasrid dynasty"), who ruled the [Emirate of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Granada "Emirate of Granada"). On multiple occasions Ibn al-Ahmar aligned himself with Ferdinand III, eventually agreeing to become his vassal in 1246.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKennedy1996276-44) Granada thereafter became a [tributary state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tributary_state "Tributary state") to the Kingdom of Castile, although this was often interrupted by wars between the two states.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKennedy1996-45)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9) The political history of the emirate was turbulent and intertwined with that of its neighbours. The Nasrids sometimes provided refuge or military aid to Castilian kings and noblemen, even against other Muslim states, while in turn the Castilians provided refuge and aid to some Nasrid emirs against other Nasrid rivals. On other occasions the Nasrids attempted to leverage the aid of the North African [Marinids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marinid_Sultanate "Marinid Sultanate") to ward off Castile, although Marinid interventions in the Peninsula ended after [Battle of Rio Salado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_R%C3%ADo_Salado "Battle of Río Salado") (1340).[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKennedy1996-45)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:8-46)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9)

The population of the emirate was also swollen by Muslim refugees from the territories newly conquered by Castile and Aragon, resulting in a small yet densely populated territory which was more uniformly Muslim and Arabic-speaking than before.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKennedy1996277-47)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey199014%E2%80%9315-48) The city itself expanded and new neighbourhoods grew around the Albaicín (named after refugees from [Baeza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baeza,_Spain "Baeza, Spain")) and in Antequeruela (named after refugees from [Antequera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antequera "Antequera") after 1410).[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKennedy1996277-47) A new set of walls was constructed further north during the 13th–14th centuries, with _Bab Ilbirah_ (present-day _Puerta de Elvira_) as its western entrance.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:24-14) A major Muslim cemetery existed outside this gate.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-49) The city's heart was its Great Mosque (on the site of the present-day [Granada Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_Cathedral "Granada Cathedral")) and the commercial district known as the _qaysariyya_ (the [Alcaicería](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcaicer%C3%ADa_of_Granada "Alcaicería of Granada")).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:24-14) Next to this was the only major [madrasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrasa "Madrasa") built in al-Andalus, the _Madrasa al-Yusufiyya_ (known today as the [Palacio de la Madraza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrasa_of_Granada "Madrasa of Granada")), founded in 1349.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBloom2020151%E2%80%93173-50)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:32-51) Other monuments from this era include the _al-Funduq al-Jadida_ ("New Inn" or [caravanserai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravanserai "Caravanserai"), now known as the [Corral del Carbón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corral_del_Carb%C3%B3n "Corral del Carbón")), built in the early 14th century,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-Capt2-52) the [Maristan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maristan_of_Granada "Maristan of Granada") (hospital), built in 1365–1367 and demolished in 1843,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:9-53) and the main mosque of the Albaicín, dating from the 13th century.[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-55)

When Ibn Al-Ahmar established himself in the city he moved the royal palace from the old Zirid citadel on the Albaicín hill to the Sabika hill, beginning construction on what became the present Alhambra.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBloom2020151-11) The Alhambra acted as a self-contained palace-city, with its own mosque, hammams, fortress, and residential quarters for workers and servants. The most celebrated palaces that survive today, such as the [Comares Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_the_Myrtles "Court of the Myrtles") and the [Palace of the Lions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_the_Lions "Court of the Lions"), generally date from the reigns of Yusuf I (r. 1333–1354) and his son Muhammad V (r. 1354–1391, with interruptions).[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBloom2020151%E2%80%93173-50) Some smaller examples of Nasrid palace architecture in the city have survived in the [Cuarto Real de Santo Domingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuarto_Real_de_Santo_Domingo "Cuarto Real de Santo Domingo") (late 13th century) and the [Dar al-Horra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dar_al-Horra "Dar al-Horra") (15th century).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEArnold2017242%E2%80%93244,_290-56)

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Granada_by_Piri_Reis.jpg/250px-Granada_by_Piri_Reis.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Granada_by_Piri_Reis.jpg)

Map showing the Emirate of Granada by Ottoman cartographer [Piri Reis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piri_Reis "Piri Reis")

Partly due to the heavy tributary payments to Castile, Granada's economy specialized in the trade of high-value goods.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9) Integrated within the European mercantile network, the ports of the kingdom fostered intense trading relations with the [Genoese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Genoa "Republic of Genoa"), but also with the Catalans, and to a lesser extent, with the Venetians, the Florentines, and the Portuguese.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-57) It provided connections with Muslim and Arab trade centres, particularly for [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold "Gold") from [sub-Saharan Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa "Sub-Saharan Africa") and the [Maghreb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maghreb "Maghreb"), and exported [silk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk "Silk") and [dried fruits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dried_fruit "Dried fruit") produced in the area.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKennedy1996277-47)

Despite its frontier position, Granada was also an important Islamic intellectual and cultural centre, especially in the time of Muhammad V, with figures such as [Ibn Khaldun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Khaldun "Ibn Khaldun") and [Ibn al-Khatib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_al-Khatib "Ibn al-Khatib") serving in the Nasrid court.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:1-42)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKennedy1996291-58)[Ibn Battuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Battuta "Ibn Battuta"), a famous traveller and historian, visited the Emirate of Granada in 1350. He described it as a powerful and self-sufficient kingdom in its own right, although frequently embroiled in skirmishes with the Kingdom of Castile. In his journal, Ibn Battuta called Granada the "metropolis of Andalusia and the bride of its cities."[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-59)

### End of Muslim rule and 16th-century changes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: End of Muslim rule and 16th-century changes")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/La_Rendici%C3%B3n_de_Granada_-_Pradilla.jpg/250px-La_Rendici%C3%B3n_de_Granada_-_Pradilla.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:La_Rendici%C3%B3n_de_Granada_-_Pradilla.jpg)

_[The Surrender of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Surrender\_of\_Granada "The Surrender of Granada")_ by F. Padilla: [Muhammad XII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_XI_of_Granada "Muhammad XI of Granada") before [Ferdinand II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_Aragon "Ferdinand II of Aragon") and [Isabella I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_I_of_Castile "Isabella I of Castile") (circa 1882)

On 2 January 1492, the last Muslim ruler in Iberia, Emir [Muhammad XI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_XI_of_Granada "Muhammad XI of Granada"), known as "Boabdil" to the Spanish, surrendered complete control of the [Emirate of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Granada "Emirate of Granada") to the [Catholic Monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Monarchs "Catholic Monarchs") ([Ferdinand II of Aragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_Aragon "Ferdinand II of Aragon") and [Isabella I of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_I_of_Castile "Isabella I of Castile")), after the last episode of the [Granada War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_War "Granada War").

The 1492 capitulation of the Kingdom of Granada to the Catholic Monarchs is one of the most significant events in Granada's history. It brought the demise of the last Muslim-controlled polity in the Iberian Peninsula. The terms of the surrender, outlined in the [Treaty of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Granada_(1491) "Treaty of Granada (1491)") at the end of 1491, explicitly allowed the Muslim inhabitants, known as _[mudéjares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar "Mudéjar")_, to continue unmolested in the practice of their faith and customs. This had been a traditional practice during Castilian (and [Aragonese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Aragon "Crown of Aragon")) conquests of Muslim cities since the takeover of [Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toledo,_Spain "Toledo, Spain") in the 11th century.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColeman201336-60) The terms of the surrender pressured Jewish inhabitants (then numbering 110 households[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-61)) to convert or leave within three years,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey1990321-62) but this provision was quickly superseded by the [Alhambra Decree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra_Decree "Alhambra Decree"), issued only a few months later on 31 March, which instead forced all Jews in Spain to convert or be expelled within four months.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColeman201338-63)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-64) Those who converted became known as _[conversos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Converso "Converso")_ (converts). This move, along with the progressive erosion of other guarantees provided by the surrender treaty, raised tensions and fears within the remaining Muslim community during the 1490s.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColeman201337%E2%80%9338-65) Many of the city's affluent Muslims and its traditional ruling classes emigrated to North Africa in the early years after the conquest, but these early emigrants numbered only a few thousand, with the rest of the population unable to afford leaving.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColeman201338-63)[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-66)

By 1499, Cardinal [Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Jim%C3%A9nez_de_Cisneros "Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros") grew frustrated with the slow pace of the efforts of the first [archbishop of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishopric_of_Granada "Archbishopric of Granada"), [Hernando de Talavera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hernando_de_Talavera "Hernando de Talavera"), to convert non-Christians and undertook a program of forced [baptisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptism "Baptism"), creating the _converso_ class for Muslims and Jews. Cisneros's new strategy, which was a direct violation of the terms of the treaty, provoked the [Rebellion of the Alpujarras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebellion_of_the_Alpujarras_(1499%E2%80%931501) "Rebellion of the Alpujarras (1499–1501)") (1499–1501) centred in the rural [Alpujarras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpujarras "Alpujarras") region southeast of the city. The rebellion lasted until 1500 in Granada and continued until 1501 in the Alpujarras.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColeman201343-67) Responding to the rebellion of 1501, the [Crown of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Castile "Crown of Castile") rescinded the Treaty of Granada,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-68) and mandated that Granada's Muslims convert or emigrate. Many of the remaining Muslim elites subsequently emigrated to North Africa. The majority of the Granada's _mudéjares_ converted (becoming the so-called _[moriscos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morisco "Morisco")_ or Moorish) so that they could stay. Both populations of converts were subject to persecution, execution, or exile, and each had cells that practiced their original religion in secrecy (the so-called _[marranos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marranos "Marranos")_ in the case of the _conversos_ accused of the charge of [crypto-Judaism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crypto-Judaism "Crypto-Judaism")).

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/Braun_Granada_HAAB.jpg/250px-Braun_Granada_HAAB.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Braun_Granada_HAAB.jpg)

16th-century view of the city, as depicted in [Georg Braun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Braun "Georg Braun")'s _Civitates orbis terrarum_

Over the course of the 16th century, Granada took on an ever more Catholic and Castilian character, as immigrants arrived from other regions of Castile, lured by the promise of economic opportunities in the newly conquered city.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColeman201315-69) At the time of the city's surrender in 1492 it had a population of 50,000 which included only a handful of Christians (mostly captives), but by 1561 (the year of the first royal [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census") of the city) the population was composed of over 30,000 Christian immigrants and approximately 15,000 _moriscos_.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColeman201315-69) After 1492 the city's first churches had been installed in some converted mosques.[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-70) The vast majority of the city's remaining mosques were subsequently converted into churches during and after the mass conversions of 1500.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColeman201396%E2%80%9397-71) In 1531, [Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") founded the [University of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Granada "University of Granada") on the site of the former madrasa built by Yusuf I.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:5-22)

Granada's Town Council did not fully establish until almost nine years after the Castilian conquest,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeinado_Santaella2013213-72) upon the concession of the so-called 'Constitutive Charter' of the Ayuntamiento of Granada on 23 September 1500.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeinado_Santaella2013221-73) From then on, the municipal institution became a crucible for the "[Old Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Christian "Old Christian")" and the converted _morisco_ elites, resulting in strong factionalism, particularly after 1508.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-74) The new period also saw the creation of a number of other new institutions such as the Cathedral Cabildo, the [Captaincy–General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captaincy%E2%80%93General_of_Granada?action=edit&redlink=1 "Captaincy–General of Granada (page does not exist)")[[es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitan%C3%ADa%20General%20de%20Granada "es:Capitanía General de Granada")], the Royal Chapel and the [Royal Chancellery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Chancellery_of_Granada "Royal Chancellery of Granada").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeinado_Santaella2013214-75) For the rest of the 16th century the Granadan ruling oligarchy featured roughly a 40% of (Jewish) _conversos_ and about a 31% of _[hidalgos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidalgo\_(nobility) "Hidalgo (nobility)")_.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeinado_Santaella2013215-76) From the 1520s onward, the mosque structures themselves began to be replaced with new church buildings, a process which continued for most of the century.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColeman201396%E2%80%9397-71) In December 1568, during a period of renewed persecution against _moriscos_, the [Second Morisco Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebellion_of_the_Alpujarras_(1568%E2%80%931571) "Rebellion of the Alpujarras (1568–1571)") broke out in the Alpujarras.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColeman20137%E2%80%938-77) Although the city's _morisco_ population played little role in the rebellion, King [Philip II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Spain "Philip II of Spain") ordered the expulsion of the vast majority of the _morisco_ population from the [Kingdom of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Granada_(Crown_of_Castile) "Kingdom of Granada (Crown of Castile)"), with the exception of those artisans and professionals judged essential to the economy. The expelled population was redistributed to other cities throughout the Crown of Castile. The [final expulsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expulsion_of_the_Moriscos "Expulsion of the Moriscos") of all _moriscos_ from Castile and Aragon was carried out between 1609 and 1614.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColeman20137%E2%80%938-77)

Early 17th-century map of Granada

During the 17th century, despite the importance of immigration,[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-78) the population of the city stagnated at about 55,000, contrary to the trend of population increase experienced in the rural areas of the [Kingdom of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Granada_(Crown_of_Castile) "Kingdom of Granada (Crown of Castile)"),[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-79) where the hammer of depopulation caused by the expulsion of the _moriscos_ had taken a far greater toll in the previous century. The 17th-century demographic stagnation in the city and overall steady population increase in the wider kingdom went in line with the demographic disaster experienced throughout the century in the rest of the Crown of Castile.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGarrido_Garc%C3%ADa200660%E2%80%9361-80) The city was overshadowed in importance by other cities including [Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville "Seville") and the capital, [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERingSalkinLa_Boda1995298-81)

Between 1810 and 1812 Granada was occupied by [Napoleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon "Napoleon")'s army during the [Peninsular War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peninsular_War "Peninsular War").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERingSalkinLa_Boda1995298-81) The French troops occupied the Alhambra as a fortified position and caused significant damage to the monument. Upon evacuating the city, they attempted to dynamite the whole complex, successfully blowing up eight towers before the remaining fuses were disabled by Spanish soldier José Garcia, thus saving what remains today.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEL%C3%B3pez2011301-82) In 1830 [Washington Irving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Irving "Washington Irving") lived in Granada and wrote his _[Tales of the Alhambra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales\_of\_the\_Alhambra "Tales of the Alhambra")_, which revived some international interest in southern Spain and in its Islamic-era monuments.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERingSalkinLa_Boda1995299-83)

In the 1930s the tensions that eventually divided Spain were evident in Granada, with frequent riots and friction between landowners and peasants. When the [Spanish Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War "Spanish Civil War") broke out in 1936, Granada was one of the cities that joined the [Nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalist_faction_(Spanish_Civil_War) "Nationalist faction (Spanish Civil War)") uprising.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERingSalkinLa_Boda1995298%E2%80%93299-84)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-85) There was local resistance against the Nationalists, particularly from the working classes in the Albaicín, which was violently repressed.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERingSalkinLa_Boda1995299-83) During the 1950s and 1960s, under the [Franco regime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francoist_Spain "Francoist Spain"), the province of Granada was one of the poorest areas in Spain.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERingSalkinLa_Boda1995299-83) In recent decades tourism has become a major industry in the city.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERingSalkinLa_Boda1995299-83)

### Location

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Location")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/%28Granada%29_Greenhouses_of_Almer%C3%ADa%2C_Spain_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-%28Granada%29_Greenhouses_of_Almer%C3%ADa%2C_Spain_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:(Granada)_Greenhouses_of_Almer%C3%ADa,_Spain_(cropped).jpg)

A satellite view centred on Granada displaying [Sierra Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Nevada_(Spain) "Sierra Nevada (Spain)") to the east and the rest of the [Vega of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vega_of_Granada "Vega of Granada"), including a number of the municipalities part of the urban area of Granada to the west

The city of Granada sits on the [Vega de Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vega_de_Granada "Vega de Granada"), one of the depressions or plains located within the [Baetic mountain ranges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baetic_System "Baetic System"), continued to the west by those of Archidona and [Antequera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoya_of_Antequera "Hoya of Antequera") and to the East by those of [Guadix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoya_of_Guadix "Hoya of Guadix"), [Baza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoya_of_Baza "Hoya of Baza") and Huéscar.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-86)

The fertile soil of the Vega, apt for agriculture, is irrigated by the water streams originated in [Sierra Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Nevada_(Spain) "Sierra Nevada (Spain)"), as well as minor secondary ranges, all drained by the catchment basin of the [Genil River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genil_River "Genil River"),[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMenor_Toribio1997192-87) that cuts across the city centre following an east to west direction. The [Monachil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monachil_(river) "Monachil (river)"), a left-bank tributary of the former, also passes through the city, discharging into the Genil to the west of the city centre.

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Climate")]

Granada has a [hot-summer Mediterranean climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot-summer_Mediterranean_climate "Hot-summer Mediterranean climate") (_Csa_) close to a cold [semi-arid climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-arid_climate "Semi-arid climate") (_BSk_). Summers are hot and dry with daily temperatures averaging 34°C (93°F) in the hottest month (July); however, temperatures reaching over 40°C (104°F) are not uncommon in the summer months. Winters are cool and damp, with most of the rainfall concentrated from November through to January. The coldest month is January with daytime temperatures hovering at 13°C (55°F) and dropping to around 1°C (34°F) during the night. Frost is common as temperatures usually reach below-freezing in the early morning. Snow is rare and occurs once every few years. Spring and autumn are unpredictable, with temperatures ranging from mild to warm. Early summer in 2017 confronted the city with two massive heat waves that broke long-standing record temperatures starting on 13 June 2017, with a new maximum high for the month at 40.6°C (old record 40.0), which was topped three times within the span of four days at 40.9°C on 14 June, 41.3 (15 June) and, eventually, 41.5 (17 June). The second extreme surge in temperatures followed roughly a month later when readings soared to 45.7 and 45.3°C on 12 and 13 July, respectively, surpassing the old July record by almost 3 degrees.

*   People older than 60 years old are 29%

### Foreign population

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Foreign population")]

As of 1 January 2025, 34,904 people living in Granada were born outside of Spain, representing 14.83% of the total population, a rate lower than the national average. Foreign-born residents originate mainly from [Latin America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America"), with the top 5 most numerous being from [Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco") (6,998), [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia") (3,252), [Venezuela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuela "Venezuela") (2,184), [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina") (1,901), and [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") (1,695).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-population-2)

**Granada** ([/ɡ r ə ˈ n ɑː d ə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_grə-NAH-də_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-8)Spanish:[[ɡɾaˈnaða]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/d/da/Pronunciation_of_Granada_in_Spanish.ogg/Pronunciation_of_Granada_in_Spanish.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pronunciation_of_Granada_in_Spanish.ogg "File:Pronunciation of Granada in Spanish.ogg")) is the [capital city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city "Capital city") of the [province of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Granada "Province of Granada"), in the [autonomous community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_communities_of_Spain "Autonomous communities of Spain") of [Andalusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusia "Andalusia"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"). Granada is located at the foot of the [Sierra Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Nevada_(Spain) "Sierra Nevada (Spain)") mountains, at the confluence of four rivers, the [Darro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darro_(river) "Darro (river)"), the [Genil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genil "Genil"), the [Monachil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monachil_(river) "Monachil (river)") and the Beiro. Ascribed to the [Vega de Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vega_de_Granada "Vega de Granada")_comarca_, the city sits at an average elevation of 738 m (2,421 ft)[above sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Above_mean_sea_level "Above mean sea level") 50 km from the [Mediterranean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean "Mediterranean") coast, the [Costa Tropical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Tropical "Costa Tropical"). With a population of 233,532 as of 2024, it is the [20th-largest city in Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_of_Spain#By_population "List of municipalities of Spain") and is an important [wine growing region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_(wine) "Granada (wine)") It was the last Muslim stronghold in Islamic Spain.

Nearby is the [Sierra Nevada Ski Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Nevada_Ski_Station "Sierra Nevada Ski Station"), where the [FIS Alpine World Ski Championships 1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIS_Alpine_World_Ski_Championships_1996 "FIS Alpine World Ski Championships 1996") were held. Its nearest airport is [Federico García Lorca Granada-Jaén Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Garc%C3%ADa_Lorca_Airport "Federico García Lorca Airport").

The area was settled since ancient times by [Iberians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberians "Iberians"), [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome"), and [Visigoths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visigothic_Kingdom "Visigothic Kingdom"). The current settlement became a major city of [Al-Andalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Andalus "Al-Andalus") in the 11th century during the [Zirid Taifa of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa_of_Granada "Taifa of Granada").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:05222-9) In the 13th century it became the capital of the [Emirate of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Granada "Emirate of Granada") under [Nasrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasrid_dynasty "Nasrid dynasty") rule, the last [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam")-ruled state in the [Iberian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula"). Granada was [conquered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_War "Granada War") in 1492 by the [Catholic Monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Monarchs_of_Spain "Catholic Monarchs of Spain") and progressively transformed into a [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians "Christians") city over the course of the 16th century.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColeman2013-10)

The [Alhambra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra "Alhambra"), a medieval Nasrid citadel and palace, is located in Granada. It is one of the most famous monuments of [Islamic architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_architecture "Islamic architecture")[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBloom2020151-11) and one of the most visited tourist sites in Spain.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-13) Islamic-period influence and [Moorish architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorish_architecture "Moorish architecture") are also preserved in the [Albaicín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albaic%C3%ADn "Albaicín") neighborhood and other medieval monuments in the city.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:24-14) The 16th century also saw a flourishing of [Mudéjar architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar_art "Mudéjar art") and [Renaissance architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_architecture "Renaissance architecture"),[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColeman201370,_89-15) followed later by [Baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque_architecture "Baroque architecture") and [Churrigueresque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Churrigueresque "Churrigueresque") styles.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-17) The [University of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Granada "University of Granada") has an estimated 47,000 undergraduate students spread over five different campuses in the city. The [pomegranate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomegranate "Pomegranate") ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _granada_) is the [heraldic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heraldry "Heraldry") device of Granada.

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

Granada's historical name in the [Arabic language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language") was غرناطة (_\_Ġarnāṭa\__).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERingSalkinLa_Boda1995296-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoom2006149-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDale1882-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEl_Hareir2011454-21) Both the name's meaning and origin are uncertain and have been debated.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:5-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:13-23) The toponym definitely existed prior to the [Zirid period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa_of_Granada "Taifa of Granada") in the 11th century.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:13-23) It probably first appeared in the 9th century[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:5-22) and it is found in Arabic sources from the 10th century.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEViguera-Mol%C3%ADns202120-24)

The word _Gárnata_ (or _Karnata_) possibly meant "hill of strangers".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-25):41[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-26) Another meaning might be "hill of pilgrims".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:5-22) It could even have been of [Berber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berber_languages "Berber languages") origin.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEViguera-Mol%C3%ADns202120-24) Another theory is that it derived from [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin")_granum_ (or its plural _grana_), meaning "seed", "beads", or a "scarlet colour", which would have been adapted into Arabic as _\_Ġarnāṭa\__ or _\_Iġranāṭa\__.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEViguera-Mol%C3%ADns202120-24) The Arab chronicler [Al-Maqqari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Maqqari "Al-Maqqari") believed that it came from the Latin word for [pomegranate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomegranate "Pomegranate"), _granata_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:5-22) In either case, the Latin word may have been used not in its primary sense, but in the more derived sense of "red", referring to the colour of the area's soil and its buildings. This would also mirror the etymology of the name of the [Alhambra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra "Alhambra").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-:13-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada#cite_note-FOOTNOTEViguera-Mol%C3%ADns202120-24)
