It was a target because of its wealth and strategic position. Founded by Francisco Fernandez de Cordoba (after whom the currency is named) in 1524 on the banks of [Lago Nicaragua](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/granada-waterfront-lago-nicaragua/), it lays claim to being the oldest city in the Americas. It was later discovered that the Rio San Juan, linking Lago Nicaragua with the Caribbean Sea, was navigable by boat, which enhanced the city’s importance as a strategic trade hub. In the 1660s, pirates used that route to launch raids on the city.

The city rebuilt but suffered again in a civil war in the 1850s when it was torched by the self-declared president of Nicaragua, American [William Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Walker_(filibuster)). That prompted yet another round of rebuilding, creating the basis of the charming city we see today.

GRANADA, Nicaragua — Pale blue and white walls frame the ornate nave of La Capilla Maria Auxiliadora (Mary Help of Christians Chapel). The chapel stands as Granada’s premier example of pure Neo-Gothic architecture, distinguished by pointed arches, verticality, and cross-ribbed vaulting that set it apart from the city’s prevailing Spanish Colonial Baroque style. Construction began in 1921 and was completed in 1922 under the guidance of Italian Salesian priest Father Jose Misieri, commemorating the first centenary of Central American independence. The hand-painted Neo-Gothic rib vaults feature a meticulous botanical catalog of 152 distinct flowers native to Nicaragua, with no two floral designs repeating across the entire ceiling. The distinctive pale blue and white color scheme reinforces the sanctuary’s Marian dedication, making the interior a remarkable expression of early 20th-century religious architecture in Nicaragua. Architect Andrés Zapata directed construction of the standing neoclassical structure, with the main facade largely complete by 1915, though the massive iron framework for the central dome did not arrive until 1916 and work continued for decades before reaching definitive completion in 1972. The official name of the cathedral is the Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption, seat of the Diocese of Granada, featuring baroque detailing across the yellow stucco exterior. ## What to know before you go

*   Granada is about a half-hour drive southeast of Managua airport (MGA / [Augusto C. Sandino International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusto_C._Sandino_International_Airport)). You can, of course, take a taxi, but most hotels can arrange a private airport pickup to take you directly, and that can work out more economical as well as more practical if you’re a larger group or have a lot of luggage. It’s also possible to take a [chicken bus](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/central-america-chicken-buses/) if you’re travelling light and trying to keep [costs to a minimum](https://www.tripadvisor.com/ShowTopic-g580113-i11278-k5124023-How_to_get_from_Managua_Airport_to_Granada-Granada_Granada_Department.html).
*   The historic old town is easily walkable (although mind the uneven sidewalks and occasional pothole). It’s also bike-friendly. If you’d prefer not to be trudging by foot through the heat of the day, taxis are easily available. There’s also the occasional tuck-tuck, and, if you’re so inclined, the horse-drawn carts next to Parque Central can take you between many of the tourist sites.
*   There’s a thriving expat scene in Granada, so there are a lot of English-speaking bars and restaurants.
*   There are also quite a few Spanish immersion schools where you can learn Spanish on location with native speakers for as long as your budget and schedule permit. They’re often surprisingly affordable, even with the optional homestay packages.
*   The tap water isn’t drinkable, but any of the bars catering to tourists will probably be using purified water for their ice, cooking, and food preparation. That said, it’s a prudent habit to ask. Bottled, purified drinking water is readily and cheaply available for purchase from street carts and stores.
*   At the time of writing, the CDC does not consider Granada city to be a malaria-risk area. But if you’re using Granada as a launching-off point for nearby areas such as the islands on the lake, those areas might be quite different. And things change, so it’s a good idea to check with a specialized travel clinic and the current [CDC recommendations for Nicaragua](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/destinations/traveler/none/nicaragua), which you can find here. Moreover, malaria isn’t the only disease mosquitoes carry; [chikungunya](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/notices/watch/chikungunya-central-america) and [dengue](https://www.cdc.gov/dengue/) are others that are common in the region.

## Notes from the field

[![Image 4: Corvina Fish Fillets Mercado de Mariscos Panama City Panama](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/10/panama-city-mercado-de-mariscos-seafood-market-in-casco-viejo-panama-city-panama-11-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Panama City’s Seafood Market (Mercado de Mariscos) PANAMA CITY, Panama — Panama isn’t an island, but with such a high proportion of coastline to land, it might as well be. So it’s only natural that seafood figures prominently in Panamanian cuisine.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/mercado-de-mariscos-panama-city/)[![Image 5: Galata Tower Galata Bridge At Dusk Istanbul Turkey](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/12/istanbul-fishermen-on-galata-bridge-istanbul-24-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Galata Bridge Has Multiple Personalities, Stacked on Top of Each Other Galata Bridge feels like it has multiple personalities: up top, cars, trams, and hundreds of fishermen crowd a bouncing deck, while down below, tourist-trap restaurants sit beside local bars watching football, all overlooking the Golden Horn.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/galata-bridge-istanbul-turkey/)[![Image 6: Iglesia San José Retablos Panama City Panama](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/10/panama-city-iglesia-san-jose-casco-viejo-panama-city-panama-23-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Iglesia San Jose, Panama City PANAMA CITY, Panama — Iglesia San José, in Casco Viejo and completed around 1675, is most famous for its massive Golden Altar (Altar de Oro). According to historical legend, the altar survived Henry Morgan’s 1671 raid when priests concealed it under black paint — though the surviving altar is dated by style to the 18th century and postdates both the raid and the city’s refounding.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/iglesia-san-jose-panama-city/)[![Image 7: Mount Kilimanjaro Sunset Above Clouds Tanzania](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/10/mt-kilimanjaro-mt-kilimanjaro-beautiful-sunset-above-the-clouds-28-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Lemosho Route Day 5: A Storm, a Glacier, and a Warning of What’s Next Overnight winds hit an estimated 50 to 60 mph, caving in tents and sending porters scrambling to anchor everything with rocks — even guides with 170 climbs said they’d never seen it last so long. Here’s how day 5 on the Lemosho Route unfolded, in words and photos, as we reached Arrow Glacier Camp beneath the Western Breach.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/climbing-kilimanjaro-lemosho-route-day-5/)[![Image 8: La Capilla Maria Auxiliadora Neo-Gothic Nave Granada Nicaragua](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/10/granada-nave-of-la-capilla-maria-auxiliadora-granada-nicaragua-21-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## La Capilla Maria Auxiliadora GRANADA, Nicaragua — La Capilla Maria Auxiliadora isn’t the grandest or most famous of Granada’s churches. But it makes a credible claim to be the most beautiful.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/capilla-maria-auxiliadora-granada-nicaragua/)[![Image 9: Metropolitan Cathedral Marble Praying Statue Santiago Chile](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/10/santiago-de-chile-metropolitan-cathedral-of-santiago-statue-09-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Santiago’s Metropolitan Cathedral SANTIAGO, Chile – The Metropolitan Cathedral has pride of place on the west side of Plaza de Armas, the historic and cultural heart of Santiago.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/metropolitan-cathedral-santiago-chile/)[![Image 10: Tikal Temple IV In Morning Mist Guatemala](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/11/tikal-tikal-mayan-ruins-and-morning-mist-08-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## The Mighty Maya City of Tikal TIKAL, Guatemala —Tikal, in northern Guatemala, was once one the largest and most powerful of the Maya cities. Today it has been most taken over by jungle.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/tikal-maya-ruins-guatemala/)[![Image 11: Dhammayazika Pagoda Golden Stupa Bagan Myanmar Landscape](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/12/bagan-pagodas-of-bagan-myanmar-39-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Dhammayazika Pagoda BAGAN, Myanmar (Burma) – Its gleaming gold stupa certainly stands out against the surrounding countryside. Completed in 1198, it features an unusual pentagonal design.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/dhammayazika-pagoda-bagan-myanmar/)[![Image 12: Sultan Selim II Tomb Interior Iznik Tiles Calligraphy Hagia Sophia Istanbul Turkey](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2017/01/istanbul-tomb-of-sultan-selim-ii-at-hagia-sophia-istanbul-turkey-02-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## The Tombs of the Sultans: Ottoman Splendor Hidden Behind Hagia Sophia Behind Hagia Sophia, a small unassuming courtyard hides five Ottoman tombs as lavish as any imperial mosque, holding sultans (some notoriously mad or drunken) buried alongside their entire families. Here’s what these opulent, little-visited chambers actually look like inside.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/hagia-sophia-tombs-sultans/)[![Image 13: One Pillar Pagoda Curved Roof Wooden Temple Hanoi Vietnam](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/11/hanoi-hanoi-one-pillar-pagoda-branches-327-0535413038-09-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## The One Pillar Pagoda, Rebuilt in Concrete The One Pillar Pagoda looks nearly a thousand years old, but the original was blown up with explosives in 1954 — an act conventionally blamed on retreating French forces — and rebuilt the following year. Despite that, it remains one of Vietnam’s most iconic Buddhist temples — here’s a firsthand look at it, lily pond and all.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/pillar-pagoda-hanoi-vietnam/)[![Image 14: Pratt Street Power Plant Brick Industrial Steel Smokestacks Baltimore USA](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2017/04/baltimore-baltimores-inner-harbor-21-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Baltimore’s Inner Harbor BALTIMORE, United States — Baltimore’s Inner Harbor is a manicured, safe, and family-friendly area of an otherwise hardscrabble city.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/baltimore-inner-harbor/)[![Image 15: Our Lady Of Pilar Church Baroque Interior Nave Buenos Aires Argentina](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/10/recoleta-our-lady-of-pilar-basilica-in-buenos-aires-agentina-17-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Our Lady of Pilar Basilica BUENOS AIRES, Argentina – Despite a checkered history, Our Lady of Pilar Basilica in Buenos Aires has survived as the second oldest church in Buenos Aires and looking none the worse for wear.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/lady-pilar-basilica-buenos-aires-argentina/)[![Image 16: Panama City Skyline From Ancon Hill Panama City Panama](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/10/panama-city-ancon-hill-panama-city-tourists-with-skyline-23-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## The View from Ancon Hill PANAMA CITY, Panama – You can spot Ancon Hill from all over Panama City. It makes for wonderful views out over Panama City and the entrance to the Panama Canal. It also has historical significance.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/ancon-hill-panama-city-panama/)[![Image 17: Topkapi Palace Imperial Council Hall Interior Istanbul](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2017/01/istanbul-topkapi-palace-imperial-council-hall-21-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Small Rooms, Huge Stakes: Topkapi’s Imperial Council Hall Just a small, ornately tiled chamber under a dome, yet this is where the Ottoman Empire’s affairs of state were decided. A golden lattice window let the Sultan secretly watch his own council meet, and its mere possibility was enough to keep the deliberations loyal.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/topkapi-palace-imperial-council-istanbul/)[![Image 18: Saucer Magnolias Enid A Haupt Garden Smithsonian Castle Washington DC](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2017/11/fijifilm-x-pro2-01-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Saucer Magnolias at the Enid Haupt Garden in Washington DC WASHINGTON DC, United States — I took this photo last spring during the very brief blooming of the tulip magnolias (or saucer magnolias) in Washington DC. They’re one of the spring’s first dramatic blooming varieties in the DC area, usually beating the more famous cherry blossoms by a couple of weeks.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/photo-of-the-saucer-magnolias-at-the-enid-haupt-garden-in-washington-dc/)[![Image 19: Panorama Of The Battle Of Waterloo Painting Waterloo Belgium](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2017/01/mont-saint-jean-panorama-of-the-battle-of-waterloo-19-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Waterloo Panorama Virtual Tour WATERLOO, Belgium — This 360° panorama captures the entire painting inside the Panorama of the Battle of Waterloo.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/waterloo-panorama-virtual-tour/)[![Image 20: Maria de Cervello Statue Patron Saint of Sailors Our Lady of Mercy Church Panama City](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/10/panama-la-iglesia-de-la-merced-casco-viejo-panama-city-statue-of-maria-de-cervello-04-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## La Iglesia de la Merced, Panama City PANAMA CITY, Panama — La Iglesia de la Merced sits in the heart of Casco Viejo, just a couple of blocks from Independence Square. The church traces its origins to 1522 and was relocated from Panama Viejo in 1673, with its stone facade reassembled at the present site following the formal refoundation of Panama City on 21 January 1673.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/iglesia-merced-panama-city/)[![Image 21: Musical Instruments Museum Decorated Harpsichord Brussels Belgium](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2017/01/brussels-musee-des-instruments-de-musique-keyboard-16-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## The Musical Instruments Museum of Brussels BRUSSELS, Belgium — The Musical Instruments Museum in Brussels has a lot to see. But it has even more to hear.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/musical-instrument-museum-brussels-belgium/)[![Image 22: Tourists at the Basilica Cistern in Istanbul, Turkey](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2023/05/istanbul-tourists-at-the-basilica-cistern-in-istanbul-turkey-10-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Not Just Any Old Water Tank: Istanbul’s Basilica Cistern It was built purely as a functional water tank for Byzantine Constantinople, yet its builders filled it with 336 recycled marble columns and two mysterious Medusa heads. Here’s a look at Istanbul’s Basilica Cistern, the underground space now nicknamed the Sunken Palace.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/basilica-cistern/)[![Image 23](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/12/sydney-sydney-city-skyline-at-dusk-03-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Sydney Harbour at Night SYDNEY, Australia — Sydney Harbour is a beautiful setting for Australia’s largest city, and at night it really sparkles.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/sydney-harbour-night-photos/)[![Image 24: Colorful Graffiti and Urban Street Art on the Streets of Lisbon, Portugal](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/10/lisbon-graffiti-in-lisbon-portugal-07-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Lisbon’s Graffiti: Bairro Alto to Belem Lisbon doesn’t come close to Athens for sheer volume of graffiti, but its downtown streets still hide some genuinely creative work. Here’s a small sampling gathered from Bairro Alto, Chiado, Rossio, the Alfama, and Belem.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/lisbon-graffiti-portugal/)[![Image 25: Royal Museums Of Fine Arts Main Hall Arches Brussels Belgium](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2017/01/brussels-brussels-royal-museums-of-fine-arts-main-hall-03-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium BRUSSELS, Belgium — Flemish art has a well-deserved reputation for its beauty. Some of the best is on display at the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium in Brussels.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/royal-museum-fine-arts-belgium-brussels/)[![Image 26: Jade Emperor Pagoda Shrine Gold Statues Incense Coils Ho Chi Minh City Vietnam](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/11/ho-chi-minh-city-jade-emperor-pagoda-ho-chi-minh-city-shrine-with-incense-07-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Inside the Tortoise Pagoda, Saigon’s Hidden Taoist Shrine Behind an unassuming gate in downtown Ho Chi Minh City sits the Jade Emperor Pagoda, a 1909 Taoist shrine also known as the Tortoise Pagoda for the turtle-filled pond by its entrance. Inside, fluorescent bulbs and candles light a crowded scene of statues and Taoist symbolism — here’s a look around.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/jade-emperor-pagoda-saigon-vietnam/)[![Image 27: King Joseph I Bronze Equestrian Statue Full Moon Praca do Comercio Lisbon Portugal](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2016/10/lisbon-king-jose-i-in-praca-do-comercio-in-lisbon-portugal-with-full-moon-12-copyright-havecamerawilltravel-com-511x288.jpg) ## Terreiro do Paço: The Palace That Became Lisbon’s Living Room Locals rarely use its formal name, Praça do Comércio — to them it’s still Terreiro do Paço, Palace Square, after the royal residence that stood here until an earthquake brought it down. From royal yellow to Republican pink and back again, here’s the story behind Lisbon’s grandest square, and what it looks like today.](https://havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/praca-do-comercio-lisbon-portugal/)

# Museo San Francisco

*   Fascinating museum in the centre of Granada
*   Housed within an old monastery
*   Famous for its collection of Zapatera statues

**Together with the [Ortiz Gurdian](https://www.beyondtheordinary.co.uk/features/ortiz-gurdian-collection/) gallery in Leon, the Museo San Francisco in [Granada](https://www.beyondtheordinary.co.uk/nicaragua-holidays/destinations/granada/) is one of the two best museums in Nicaragua and highly recommended.**

![Image 4: Museo Convento San Francisco Granada](https://www.beyondtheordinary.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/Museo-Convento-San-Francisco-Granada.jpg)

Also commonly known as the Museo del Convento de San Francisco, this is something of a double-header as a visitor attraction.

The beautiful church of San Francisco, one of the oldest in Granada (dating back to the 16 th century, although the structure you see today dates back to the late 19 th century), still functions as a place of worship, is free to visit and well worth your time.

Adjoining the church is the old monastery (convento is the Spanish word for a monastery) which now serves as an excellent museum.

Quite aside from the exhibits, half of the charm of the Museo San Francisco is its beautiful setting and graceful, monastic architecture, specifically its elegant, open air cloister.

![Image 5: Sculpture Granada Museum](https://www.beyondtheordinary.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/Sculpture-Granada-Museum.jpg)

In terms of the exhibits, the main part of the museum houses a collection of modern and primitive art and sculpture, some of it religious in theme, some not.

However, the Museo San Francisco is principally famous for its collection of giant Zapatera statues that are lined up in avenue formation in the gardens at the back of the museum.

These statues take their name from the nearby island of Zapatera where they were discovered in the 1880s.

Although relatively little is known about the Pre-Columbian people that inhabited the region, it is widely assumed that the entire island of Zapatera held some form of religious / ritual significance, rather than a place where people lived.

![Image 6](https://www.beyondtheordinary.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/atol-11532.png.webp)**Beyond The Ordinary arrange fully bonded, tailor made holidays and tours to Nicaragua. Contact one of our experts on 01580 764796, email [travel@beyondtheordinary.co.uk](mailto:travel@beyondtheordinary.co.uk) or contact us via [our website.](https://www.beyondtheordinary.co.uk/contact/)**
* * *

Quite apart from the varied exhibits, the Museo San Francisco receives surprisingly few visitors and is therefore, for the most part, a wonderfully peaceful place to sit and soak up some colonial atmosphere.

Our suggestion is always to book a morning walking tour of Granada, break for lunch and then visit the museum in the afternoon.

For holiday ideas that include Granada, we suggest visiting our [Itineraries](https://www.beyondtheordinary.co.uk/nicaragua-holidays/itineraries/) page while, for hotels in Granada, please visit our [Accommodation](https://www.beyondtheordinary.co.uk/nicaragua-holidays/accommodation/granada/) page.

# Museo San Francisco

*   Fascinating museum in the centre of Granada
*   Housed within an old monastery
*   Famous for its collection of Zapatera statues

**Together with the [Ortiz Gurdian](https://www.beyondtheordinary.co.uk/features/ortiz-gurdian-collection/) gallery in Leon, the Museo San Francisco in [Granada](https://www.beyondtheordinary.co.uk/nicaragua-holidays/destinations/granada/) is one of the two best museums in Nicaragua and highly recommended.**

![Image 4: Museo Convento San Francisco Granada](https://www.beyondtheordinary.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/Museo-Convento-San-Francisco-Granada.jpg)

Also commonly known as the Museo del Convento de San Francisco, this is something of a double-header as a visitor attraction.

The beautiful church of San Francisco, one of the oldest in Granada (dating back to the 16 th century, although the structure you see today dates back to the late 19 th century), still functions as a place of worship, is free to visit and well worth your time.

Adjoining the church is the old monastery (convento is the Spanish word for a monastery) which now serves as an excellent museum.

Quite aside from the exhibits, half of the charm of the Museo San Francisco is its beautiful setting and graceful, monastic architecture, specifically its elegant, open air cloister.

![Image 5: Sculpture Granada Museum](https://www.beyondtheordinary.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/Sculpture-Granada-Museum.jpg)

In terms of the exhibits, the main part of the museum houses a collection of modern and primitive art and sculpture, some of it religious in theme, some not.

However, the Museo San Francisco is principally famous for its collection of giant Zapatera statues that are lined up in avenue formation in the gardens at the back of the museum.

These statues take their name from the nearby island of Zapatera where they were discovered in the 1880s.

Although relatively little is known about the Pre-Columbian people that inhabited the region, it is widely assumed that the entire island of Zapatera held some form of religious / ritual significance, rather than a place where people lived.

![Image 6](https://www.beyondtheordinary.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/atol-11532.png.webp)**Beyond The Ordinary arrange fully bonded, tailor made holidays and tours to Nicaragua. Contact one of our experts on 01580 764796, email [travel@beyondtheordinary.co.uk](mailto:travel@beyondtheordinary.co.uk) or contact us via [our website.](https://www.beyondtheordinary.co.uk/contact/)**
* * *

Quite apart from the varied exhibits, the Museo San Francisco receives surprisingly few visitors and is therefore, for the most part, a wonderfully peaceful place to sit and soak up some colonial atmosphere.

Our suggestion is always to book a morning walking tour of Granada, break for lunch and then visit the museum in the afternoon.

## Colonial city with volcano views

Granada isn’t a colonial capital, but it is the oldest colonial city in Nicaragua and one of the oldest in Central America. This small, lakeside city acts as a transit hub of sorts, connecting to adventures throughout the country, like Ometepe island. Those who use Granada as a home base will find tons of things to do, like satiating a sweet tooth at the Chocolate Museum, munching on traditional Nicaraguan street food straight out of a local’s kitchen window, and watching the sunrise over the lake on the malecon.

[Why you are seeing these recommendations](https://www.viator.com/support/siteoperation)

## Top 15 attractions in Granada

[![Image 2: Granada Cathedral](https://dynamic-media.tacdn.com/media/photo-o/34/26/39/41/caption.jpg?w=2400&h=-1&s=1) #1 4.9 (725) ### Granada Cathedral The Granada Cathedral rises above the city skyline in a vision of red domes and lemon-yellow walls backed by the towering Mombacho volcano. Well recognized for its beauty, the Spanish Renaissance cathedral—whose first stone was laid in 1523 and took 181 years to complete—is a quintessential image of Nicaragua and a popular Granada attraction. ...More](https://www.viator.com/Granada-attractions/Granada-Cathedral/d4853-a15130)

[![Image 3: Smoking Masaya Volcano perched between Managua and Granada.](https://dynamic-media.tacdn.com/media/photo-o/32/50/a9/89/caption.jpg?w=2400&h=-1&s=1) #2 4.7 (972) ### Masaya Volcano Skip the hike and drive right up to the lava-spitting rim of Masaya Volcano (Volcan Masaya), perched between Managua and Granada. The active volcano’s famous lava shows at the Santiago Crater, combined with ridiculously easy access, have made it one of the most popular attractions in all of Nicaragua. ...More](https://www.viator.com/Managua-attractions/Masaya-Volcano/d4500-a6928)

[![Image 4: Catarina](https://dynamic-media.tacdn.com/media/photo-o/34/26/3a/3b/caption.jpg?w=2400&h=-1&s=1) #3 4.8 (888) ### Catarina Catarina is a colorful Nicaraguan village overflowing with so many flowers that these friendly florals outnumber the locals. Throughout the town, you’ll find gardens, nurseries, and flower baskets handwoven by Catarina’s skilled artisans. Catarina is a breath of fresh air for travelers looking to escape Nicaragua’s busy cities. ...More](https://www.viator.com/Nicaragua-attractions/Catarina/d4499-a15038)

[![Image 5: Lake Nicaragua (Lake Cocibolca)](https://dynamic-media.tacdn.com/media/photo-o/34/25/b9/d3/caption.jpg?w=2400&h=-1&s=1) #4 4.9 (823) ### Lake Nicaragua (Lake Cocibolca) Lake Nicaragua (also known as Lake Cocibolca) is Central America’s largest lake and an outdoor activity destination for locals and visitors alike. Nature lovers will enjoy bird watching from the shore, boating to the lake’s islands, or hiking the island’s volcanoes. Plus the cities around Lake Nicaragua offer many archeological sites, historic churches, and local markets to explore. ...More](https://www.viator.com/Nicaragua-attractions/Lake-Nicaragua-Lake-Cocibolca/d4499-a6939)

[![Image 6: Masaya](https://dynamic-media.tacdn.com/media/photo-o/34/26/39/9f/caption.jpg?w=2400&h=-1&s=1) #5 4.9 (115) ### Masaya The city of Masaya showcases Nicaragua's Spanish and Indigenous cultures among its historic plazas and lakeside promenade. Known as the Cradle of National Folklore, Masaya sees the streets taken over by traditional dancers for a “Night of Revelry” (Noche de Verbena) every Thursday. Just beyond the city limits, you’ll find the smoldering Masaya Volcano. ...More](https://www.viator.com/Nicaragua-attractions/Masaya/d4499-a15039)

[![Image 7: Islets of Granada (Las Isletas de Granada)](https://dynamic-media.tacdn.com/media/photo-o/34/25/b9/71/caption.jpg?w=2400&h=-1&s=1) #6 4.7 (71) ### Islets of Granada (Las Isletas de Granada) Lake Nicaragua, Central America’s largest lake, is home to an archipelago of 365 islands. Formed by the eruption of Mombacho Volcano, the Islets of Granada include uninhabited isles, traditional fishing villages, private residences, and luxurious resorts. Explore as part of a “best of” Nicaragua or Granada tour, or with a private guide. ...More](https://www.viator.com/Nicaragua-attractions/Islets-of-Granada-Las-Isletas-de-Granada/d4499-a6931)

[![Image 8: Apoyo Lagoon Natural Reserve (Laguna de Apoyo)](https://dynamic-media.tacdn.com/media/photo-o/34/26/1b/53/caption.jpg?w=2400&h=-1&s=1) #7 4.6 (55) ### Apoyo Lagoon Natural Reserve (Laguna de Apoyo) A crystalline lagoon just a short drive from Granada, Apoyo Lagoon Natural Reserve (Reserva Natural Laguna de Apoyo) is one of the most popular natural attractions in Nicaragua. Get away from the city for a few hours of kid-approved water sports, or hang out and relax all day in a lounge chair poised on the rim of this beautiful crater lake. ...More](https://www.viator.com/Granada-attractions/Apoyo-Lagoon-Natural-Reserve-Laguna-de-Apoyo/d4853-a13558)

[![Image 9: Mombacho Volcano](https://dynamic-media.tacdn.com/media/photo-o/34/26/a9/8e/caption.jpg?w=2400&h=-1&s=1) #8 4.8 (58) ### Mombacho Volcano With an Aztec name that translates to “Steep Mountain,” the Mombacho volcano certainly lives up to its name. Its 4,410-foot (1,344-meter) peak towers over Nicaragua’s colonial city of Granada, creating both a beautiful backdrop and a huge backyard ripe for adventure and exploration. ...More](https://www.viator.com/Granada-attractions/Mombacho-Volcano/d4853-a17240)

[![Image 10: Iglesia de la Merced](https://dynamic-media.tacdn.com/media/photo-o/34/25/b9/c2/caption.jpg?w=2400&h=-1&s=1) #9 4.9 (79) ### Iglesia de la Merced There are several churches in Granada to visit, but the Iglesia de la Merced, not far from Parque Central (Central Park), is noted by many as the city's most beautiful. The church on this site dates from the early 16th century, although it has been damaged twice (to the point of nearly-complete destruction once) and rebuilt, most recently in the 1860s. ...More](https://www.viator.com/Granada-attractions/Iglesia-de-la-Merced/d4853-a6932)

[![Image 11: House of Three Worlds (Casa de los Tres Mundos)](https://dynamic-media.tacdn.com/media/photo-o/34/26/38/50/caption.jpg?w=2400&h=-1&s=1) #10 5.0 (3) ### House of Three Worlds (Casa de los Tres Mundos) House of the Three Worlds (Casa de los Tres Mundos), a nonprofit arts and cultural organization in Granada, is housed in a former colonial mansion. It hosts a variety of artistic showcases including film screenings, poetry readings, and dance performances. Both local and international acts visit this venue in Nicaragua. ...More](https://www.viator.com/Nicaragua-attractions/House-of-Three-Worlds-Casa-de-los-Tres-Mundos/d4499-a15129)

[![Image 12: Calle La Calzada](https://dynamic-media.tacdn.com/media/photo-o/34/27/19/80/caption.jpg?w=2400&h=-1&s=1) #11 5.0 (10) ### Calle La Calzada Stroll down Calle La Calzada after dark to see why this street is the heart of Granada’s nightlife: live music blasts from bars, outdoor tables overflow with revelers, and artisans hawk their wares. During the day, the street is a main thoroughfare with shopping and dining venues in Spanish colonial buildings—it’s impossible to miss. ...More](https://www.viator.com/Granada-attractions/Calle-La-Calzada/d4853-a21643)

[![Image 13: Mi Museo](https://dynamic-media.tacdn.com/media/photo-o/34/25/b7/78/caption.jpg?w=2400&h=-1&s=1) #12 0.0 (0) ### Mi Museo Spend an hour learning about pre-Columbian Nicaragua on a visit to Mi Museo, a small and privately owned collection of artifacts. Not only is this Granada museum a great introduction to Nicaragua’s diverse indigenous cultures and histories, but it’s also very low cost, making it a quick and easy destination to tick off your sightseeing list. ...More](https://www.viator.com/Granada-attractions/Mi-Museo/d4853-a6935)

With a history dating back to 1529, it's among the oldest churches in Nicaragua and remains one of Granada’s most memorable sights. ...More](https://www.viator.com/Granada-attractions/San-Francisco-Convent-Iglesia-de-San-Francisco/d4853-a6934)

[![Image 15: Hacienda El Progreso](https://dynamic-media.tacdn.com/media/photo-o/34/26/b3/68/caption.jpg?w=2400&h=-1&s=1) #14 0.0 (0) ### Hacienda El Progreso On the forested flanks of Mombacho volcano, high above the cobbled streets of the colonial city of Granada, the family-run Hacienda El Progreso is where Nicaraguan coffee was born. This coffee plantation and ecotourism hot spot is best known as a lead supplier for Nicaragua’s biggest coffee chain, Café las Flores. ...More](https://www.viator.com/Granada-attractions/Hacienda-El-Progreso/d4853-a17681)

[![Image 16: La Polvora Fortress (Fortaleza La Polvora)](https://dynamic-media.tacdn.com/media/photo-o/34/25/b7/91/caption.jpg?w=2400&h=-1&s=1) #15 0.0 (0) ### La Polvora Fortress (Fortaleza La Polvora) Originally built by the Spanish in the 1740s as a fort to ward off pirates, today the Fortaleza La Polvora is a military museum and popular tourist stop in Granada. This sturdy medieval fortress consists of several lookout towers connected by stone walls with a huge arched main gate and the views from the tower make it worth the visit. ...More](https://www.viator.com/Nicaragua-attractions/Fortaleza-La-Polvora/d4499-a6936)

When to visit

Nicaragua’s dry season (November–May) is typically the time to visit. Don’t let rain storms deter you from exploring in summer and fall. Storms can complicate some trips out of the city, but indoor Granada activities include the Chocolate Museum, House of the Three Worlds (Casa de los Tres Mundos), and San Francisco Convent (Iglesia de San Francisco).

Getting around

Getting around Granada is easy: Walk to your destination. You can explore on foot easily in this walkable city. The main tourist attractions (museums, churches, scenic spots) are assembled within a few minutes of each other. The critical element is to know how to get to and from Granada. Private and shared shuttles are more expensive and tend to follow a specific schedule. Public transportation like chicken buses may be more frequent, but they fill up quickly.

Traveler tips

Travelers are often advised to avoid visiting in the rainy season because back roads get flooded, trails get muddy, and lightning sightings can ruin a beach trip. If you take advantage of the smaller crowds in the rainy season, plan around the rain, including the days after. For instance, the Telica volcano is a popular hike with an over-the-rim view, but when the day prior’s forecast included rain, a sulfuric mist obscures visibility into the crater.

People Also Ask**Q:**Why do people go to Granada, Nicaragua?

**A:**

People visit Granada, Nicaragua, to see its colonial architecture and to take day trips to other popular sites. Granada is a popular overnight spot for backpackers who plan on visiting Ometepe island, San Juan del Sur’s beaches, Masaya’s volcano and markets, and Mombacho’s dormant volcano.

**Q:**How far is Granada, Nicaragua, from the beach?

**A:**

Granada borders Lake Cocibolca, but its shoreline is better for kayaking and boating to Ometepe’s beaches. For a proper ocean or sea beach, one of the most popular to visit from Granada is San Juan del Sur, a 2-hour drive south on the Pacific coast.

**Q:**Is it walkable in Granada?

**A:**

Yes, Granada is a walkable city. If you’re in the city's central area, such as around Parque Central de Granada, you can safely walk to multiple attractions within five to 15 minutes. Generally, walking around at night is safe, though many streets are quiet as businesses close.

**Q:**What food is Granada known for?

**A:**

Granada is a great place to try traditional Nicaraguan food. _Vigorón_ is especially good in Granada, as are staples like _gallo pinto_ and _habas con jamon._ Many locals sell food out of their kitchen windows, so try an amazing _nacatamal_ for an unbelievable price.

**Q:**What is the most Instagrammable place in Granada, Nicaragua?

**A:**

Like in many Spanish colonial cities in Central America, some of the most Instagrammable places in Granada are where the Immaculate Conception of Mary Cathedral Church is a backdrop. This yellow church on the Central Square is the city's postcard landmark and one of the best backdrops for photos.

**Q:**How long should I stay in Granada Nicaragua?

**A:**

Visitors tend to visit Granada, Nicaragua, in one of two ways: either with an overnight stay or two or as a home base for exploring other areas of Nicaragua. There’s plenty to do in the area, like visiting the markets in Masaya, kayaking around Ometepe island, and hiking Mombacho Volcano.

## Colonial city with volcano views

Granada isn’t a colonial capital, but it is the oldest colonial city in Nicaragua and one of the oldest in Central America. This small, lakeside city acts as a transit hub of sorts, connecting to adventures throughout the country, like Ometepe island. Those who use Granada as a home base will find tons of things to do, like satiating a sweet tooth at the Chocolate Museum, munching on traditional Nicaraguan street food straight out of a local’s kitchen window, and watching the sunrise over the lake on the malecon.

When to visit

Nicaragua’s dry season (November–May) is typically the time to visit. Don’t let rain storms deter you from exploring in summer and fall. Storms can complicate some trips out of the city, but indoor Granada activities include the Chocolate Museum, House of the Three Worlds (Casa de los Tres Mundos), and San Francisco Convent (Iglesia de San Francisco).

Getting around

Getting around Granada is easy: Walk to your destination. You can explore on foot easily in this walkable city. The main tourist attractions (museums, churches, scenic spots) are assembled within a few minutes of each other. The critical element is to know how to get to and from Granada. Private and shared shuttles are more expensive and tend to follow a specific schedule. Public transportation like chicken buses may be more frequent, but they fill up quickly.

Traveler tips

Travelers are often advised to avoid visiting in the rainy season because back roads get flooded, trails get muddy, and lightning sightings can ruin a beach trip. If you take advantage of the smaller crowds in the rainy season, plan around the rain, including the days after. For instance, the Telica volcano is a popular hike with an over-the-rim view, but when the day prior’s forecast included rain, a sulfuric mist obscures visibility into the crater.

People Also Ask**Q:**Why do people go to Granada, Nicaragua?

**A:**

People visit Granada, Nicaragua, to see its colonial architecture and to take day trips to other popular sites. Granada is a popular overnight spot for backpackers who plan on visiting Ometepe island, San Juan del Sur’s beaches, Masaya’s volcano and markets, and Mombacho’s dormant volcano.

**Q:**How far is Granada, Nicaragua, from the beach?

**A:**

Granada borders Lake Cocibolca, but its shoreline is better for kayaking and boating to Ometepe’s beaches. For a proper ocean or sea beach, one of the most popular to visit from Granada is San Juan del Sur, a 2-hour drive south on the Pacific coast.

**Q:**Is it walkable in Granada?

**A:**

Yes, Granada is a walkable city. If you’re in the city's central area, such as around Parque Central de Granada, you can safely walk to multiple attractions within five to 15 minutes. Generally, walking around at night is safe, though many streets are quiet as businesses close.

**Q:**What food is Granada known for?

**A:**

Granada is a great place to try traditional Nicaraguan food. _Vigorón_ is especially good in Granada, as are staples like _gallo pinto_ and _habas con jamon._ Many locals sell food out of their kitchen windows, so try an amazing _nacatamal_ for an unbelievable price.

**Q:**What is the most Instagrammable place in Granada, Nicaragua?

**A:**

Like in many Spanish colonial cities in Central America, some of the most Instagrammable places in Granada are where the Immaculate Conception of Mary Cathedral Church is a backdrop. This yellow church on the Central Square is the city's postcard landmark and one of the best backdrops for photos.

**Q:**How long should I stay in Granada Nicaragua?

**A:**

Visitors tend to visit Granada, Nicaragua, in one of two ways: either with an overnight stay or two or as a home base for exploring other areas of Nicaragua. There’s plenty to do in the area, like visiting the markets in Masaya, kayaking around Ometepe island, and hiking Mombacho Volcano.

**Granada** (Spanish pronunciation:[[ɡɾaˈnaða]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) is a city in western [Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua "Nicaragua") and the capital of the [Granada Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_Department "Granada Department"). With an estimated population of 105,862 (2022),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-2) it is Nicaragua's ninth most populous city. Granada is historically one of Nicaragua's most important cities, economically and politically. It has a rich colonial heritage, seen in its architecture and structure.

Granada had a thriving indigenous population. In 1524, the city was renamed Granada, by [Francisco Hernández de Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Hern%C3%A1ndez_de_C%C3%B3rdoba_(founder_of_Nicaragua) "Francisco Hernández de Córdoba (founder of Nicaragua)"), ostensibly the first European city in mainland America. Unlike other cities that claim the same distinction, the city of Granada was not only the settlement of the conquest, but also a city registered in official records of the Crown of Aragon, and the Kingdom of Castile in Spain.

Granada is also known as _La Gran Sultana_, in the reflection of its Moorish and Andalusian appearance, unlike its sister city and historical rival [León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n_(Nicaragua) "León (Nicaragua)"), which displays Castilian trends.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/GranadaNicaragua1900.jpg/250px-GranadaNicaragua1900.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GranadaNicaragua1900.jpg)

Granada street scene, circa 1905

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Old_Market_Building_of_Granada%2C_Nicaragua_in_1880.jpg/250px-Old_Market_Building_of_Granada%2C_Nicaragua_in_1880.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Old_Market_Building_of_Granada,_Nicaragua_in_1880.jpg)

Old Market Building of Granada in 1880

The settlement of Granada was established by Spanish conquistador [Hernández de Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Hern%C3%A1ndez_de_C%C3%B3rdoba_(founder_of_Nicaragua) "Francisco Hernández de Córdoba (founder of Nicaragua)"), who named it after the city of the same name in Spain. This was done in honor of [the city's capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_War "Granada War") by the forces of [King Ferdinand II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_Aragon "Ferdinand II of Aragon") and [Queen Isabella I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_I_of_Castile "Isabella I of Castile") from the [Emirate of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Granada "Emirate of Granada"), which completed the _[reconquista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista "Reconquista")_. During the colonial era, Granada was a [sister city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sister_city "Sister city") to the settlement of [Antigua Guatemala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antigua_Guatemala "Antigua Guatemala"), maintained a flourishing level of commerce with ports in the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") via [Lake Cocibolca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua") and the [San Juan River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juan_River_(Nicaragua) "San Juan River (Nicaragua)"), and was subject to attacks from [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_people "English people"), [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people "French people") and [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_people "Dutch people")[pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piracy_in_the_Caribbean "Piracy in the Caribbean") who unsuccessfully attempted to take control of the settlement by sailing up the San Juan River.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-3)

For many years Granada disputed with [León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n,_Nicaragua "León, Nicaragua") its hegemony as the major city of Nicaragua. The city of Granada was favored by the [Conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism "Conservatism"), while Léon was favored by the [Liberals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism "Liberalism"). For many years there was conflict that at times became quite violent between the cities' families and political factions. In the mid-19th century a compromise site was agreed on and the capital was finally established at [Managua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managua "Managua") between both cities.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] As of 1850, Granada had a population of approximately 10,000.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-Baily-4)

On 29 May 1834, [Cándido Flores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A1ndido_Flores?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cándido Flores (page does not exist)"), head of the military forces of Granada, revolted against the Government in [León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n,_Nicaragua "León, Nicaragua") led by [José Núñez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_N%C3%BA%C3%B1ez_(President_of_Nicaragua) "José Núñez (President of Nicaragua)"), demanding the reform of the federal Constitution. After being defeated in Managua he could not organize a resistance in Granada, so he left the city to a disorganized mob that committed lootings and robberies, especially in the houses of foreigners.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-5)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/General_Walker_Reviewing_Troops_on_the_Grand_Plaza%2C_Granada%2C_Capital_of_Nicaragua_-_FL_1856.jpg/250px-General_Walker_Reviewing_Troops_on_the_Grand_Plaza%2C_Granada%2C_Capital_of_Nicaragua_-_FL_1856.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:General_Walker_Reviewing_Troops_on_the_Grand_Plaza,_Granada,_Capital_of_Nicaragua_-_FL_1856.jpg)

American-born General William [Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Walker_(filibuster) "William Walker (filibuster)") reviewing his troops on the Grand Plaza, Granada, capital of Nicaragua. Illustration for Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper, June 21 of 1856.

Granada was also the site where American [filibuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filibuster_(military) "Filibuster (military)")[William Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Walker_(filibuster) "William Walker (filibuster)") took up residence and attempted to take control of [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America") and create independent colonies with economies based on slavery. One of Walker's generals, [Charles Frederick Henningsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Frederick_Henningsen "Charles Frederick Henningsen"), set the city ablaze before escaping, destroying much of the colonial-era architecture and inscribed the words "Here was Granada" on the ruins before he left.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-7)

Granada avoided much of the tumult of the [Sandinista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandinista "Sandinista") Era in the 1970–80s.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/St_Francis_Church_Granada_Nicaragua.jpg/250px-St_Francis_Church_Granada_Nicaragua.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_Francis_Church_Granada_Nicaragua.jpg)

San Francisco Convent Church, built in 1685-late 18th century by the [Franciscans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franciscans "Franciscans").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-10)

Granada is located along the coast of the [Lake Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua") (a.k.a. Lake Cocibolca), the world's twentieth largest lake.

Physiographically, the city occupies a low-lying alluvial terrace within the Nicaraguan Depression (or Central Nicaraguan Graben), bounded by the volcanic flanks of [Mombacho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombacho "Mombacho") to the south and the tectonic basin of [Lake Cocibolca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua") to the east.

Granada is the capital city of the Department of Granada, which borders Boaco and [Managua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managua "Managua") to the north, Masaya and Carazo to the east and Rivas to the south. Within the same department, the River Tipitapa which connects the Lake of Managua and Nicaragua passes through it in the north. It also has three volcanic lagoons; Manares, Genirzaro, and the famous Apoyo. Apoyo, which is shared with the Department of Masaya, is the largest volcanic lagoon in Nicaragua.

Granada is a very warm city all year round, with very similar temperatures to Managua. This is due to similarities in geography with its close proximity to a lake and surrounded by high hills. Rainfall in Granada is approximately between 1,100 and 2,100 mm annually, with an annual average temperature reported to be 25.7°C. [[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-11)

The vegetation around Granada is a reflection of its climatology. Dry and humid forests skirt the [Mombacho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombacho "Mombacho") volcano. The volcano is also home to a wide array of [fauna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna "Fauna")_(See [Wildlife of Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildlife\_of\_Nicaragua "Wildlife of Nicaragua"))_. The lake is also home to many creatures, both marine and freshwater creatures. It is the only freshwater lake in the world where sharks live ([Nicaragua shark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua_shark "Nicaragua shark")). Fishing in the lake is quite good, and fishermen, both commercial and recreational, regularly catch [guapote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parachromis "Parachromis") and [mojarras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mojarra "Mojarra"), as well as [sardines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardine "Sardine"). Nicaragua has recently banned fishing of the Nicaragua shark and [sawfish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sawfish "Sawfish") because of population decline.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-12)

Other cities and towns within the Granada district include Malacatoya, El Paso, El Guayabo, Diria, Macatepe, El Guanacaste, [Nandaime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandaime "Nandaime") and Diriomo, known nationally as the last city of witches. Mombacho volcano is the highest point (1,345 m) within Granada; the now dormant volcano blew most of its cone into the lake, forming the 365 [Islets of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islets_of_Granada "Islets of Granada"). It is also possible on a clear day to see [Ometepe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ometepe "Ometepe") and [Zapatera Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zapatera_Island "Zapatera Island").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The later island is the second largest island in [Lake Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua"), and also harbors an inactive volcano. The largest is Ometepe Island, also located in Lake Nicaragua. Several [pre-Columbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian "Pre-Columbian") statues and idols were found on the island during the [Spanish conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest "Spanish conquest"), and now exhibited in the Convento San Francisco Museum, as well as in other museums and parks located on Ometepe Island.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-13)

Granada has several beaches on Lake Nicaragua which are very popular around [Semana Santa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semana_Santa "Semana Santa") ("Holy Week").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Granada%2C_Nicaragua_4.jpg/250px-Granada%2C_Nicaragua_4.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Granada,_Nicaragua_4.jpg)

Xalteva Church, it was originally built during colonial times and due to its location it was used as a military fortress. The façade and interior were rebuilt after its destruction by [William Walker the filibuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Walker_(filibuster) "William Walker (filibuster)"), it was finally rebuilt in 1890–1898.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-18)

Granada has long been a center of commerce, including [timber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timber "Timber"), [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold "Gold") and [silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver "Silver"). Granada's economy continues to grow as it is becoming a hub for tourism. Though Granada remains Nicaragua's sixth largest city, it is widely known for preserving some of the finest colonial-era architecture in the country.

A real estate boom had been underway for several years, with many European and Americans purchasing and renovating the area's homes for retirement or holiday homes and several foreign realtors establishing offices, but that boom slowed in 2007. The prior escalation of real estate prices in Granada and other parts of Southwestern Nicaragua has led to a shift of investor attention toward Northern Nicaragua and the cities of [Matagalpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matagalpa "Matagalpa"), Leon, [Corinto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corinto,_Nicaragua "Corinto, Nicaragua") and the surrounding beaches of Leon and Corinto.

Museums have opened, and new hotels and restaurants are proliferating at a fast rate.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Granada, though now dependent on tourism, also has fertile agricultural land within the municipality. Major production of organic [coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee "Coffee") and [cacao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocoa_bean "Cocoa bean"), [cattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cattle "Cattle"), [plantains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plantain_(cooking) "Plantain (cooking)") and [bananas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banana "Banana") occurs within its boundaries.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Gastronomy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Gastronomy")]

See also: [Tourism in Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Nicaragua "Tourism in Nicaragua")

Granada's restaurants have received recognition by newspapers like the New York Times.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-19) In the city of Granada, there are a number of restaurants including Pita Pita, Garden Café & La Hacienda. In recent years,[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] the city of Granada's evolving culinary scene mixes local and international flavors, as well as supporting [farm-to-table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farm-to-table "Farm-to-table") sustainability of local growers and producers.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Granada's economy continues to grow in big part because it has become a tourist attraction for its colonial architecture, as well as its ecology and now as a food destination.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-20)

## Infrastructure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Infrastructure")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Typical_Nicaraguan_street.JPG/250px-Typical_Nicaraguan_street.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Typical_Nicaraguan_street.JPG)

A street of Granada

Most of Granada's streets are narrow, as the city evolved centuries before the advent of motorized vehicles. Therefore, today, many streets allow only one-way traffic, offering a challenge to visitors traveling by car.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Following many years of neglect, primarily due to the economic collapse of the nation in the 1980s, most of Granada's buildings and [infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure "Infrastructure") began to deteriorate. Roads and public utilities fell into disrepair.

In the decades that followed, however, the city government directed funds towards recognition and [restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_restoration "Building restoration") of many of Granada's historic structures. The Spanish government has provided financial cooperation for the refurbishment of the city. One such project is transforming Calle La Calzada into a pedestrian street.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-21)

## Culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Culture")]

See also: [Culture of Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_Nicaragua "Culture of Nicaragua")

Granada, like most of the Nicaraguan Pacific, is populated primarily by a Spanish-speaking majority of [Mestizos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo"). Residing here also are people from the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland"), [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria"), the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), and [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France").

Until recently, Nicaragua was experiencing a booming tourist economy. This, in turn, attracted foreigners to Granada seeking colonial homes for purchase, adding a growing number of Europeans and Americans to the city's population. Real estate prices had increased following the foreign interest and subsequent investments. However, with the 2018 civil conflict, the US Department of State issued a travel advisory, citing "civil unrest, crime, limited healthcare availability, and arbitrary enforcement of laws."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-22) In 2020, it issued a Level 4, "Do Not Travel" advisory due to COVID-19.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-23) The city is recognized as a "[Design City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_Cities_(UNESCO) "Design Cities (UNESCO)")" by [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")'s [Creative Cities Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Cities_Network "Creative Cities Network").

**Granada** (Spanish pronunciation:[[ɡɾaˈnaða]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) is a city in western [Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua "Nicaragua") and the capital of the [Granada Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_Department "Granada Department"). With an estimated population of 105,862 (2022),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-2) it is Nicaragua's ninth most populous city. Granada is historically one of Nicaragua's most important cities, economically and politically. It has a rich colonial heritage, seen in its architecture and structure.

Granada had a thriving indigenous population. In 1524, the city was renamed Granada, by [Francisco Hernández de Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Hern%C3%A1ndez_de_C%C3%B3rdoba_(founder_of_Nicaragua) "Francisco Hernández de Córdoba (founder of Nicaragua)"), ostensibly the first European city in mainland America. Unlike other cities that claim the same distinction, the city of Granada was not only the settlement of the conquest, but also a city registered in official records of the Crown of Aragon, and the Kingdom of Castile in Spain.

Granada is also known as _La Gran Sultana_, in the reflection of its Moorish and Andalusian appearance, unlike its sister city and historical rival [León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n_(Nicaragua) "León (Nicaragua)"), which displays Castilian trends.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/GranadaNicaragua1900.jpg/250px-GranadaNicaragua1900.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GranadaNicaragua1900.jpg)

Granada street scene, circa 1905

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Old_Market_Building_of_Granada%2C_Nicaragua_in_1880.jpg/250px-Old_Market_Building_of_Granada%2C_Nicaragua_in_1880.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Old_Market_Building_of_Granada,_Nicaragua_in_1880.jpg)

Old Market Building of Granada in 1880

The settlement of Granada was established by Spanish conquistador [Hernández de Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Hern%C3%A1ndez_de_C%C3%B3rdoba_(founder_of_Nicaragua) "Francisco Hernández de Córdoba (founder of Nicaragua)"), who named it after the city of the same name in Spain. This was done in honor of [the city's capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_War "Granada War") by the forces of [King Ferdinand II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_Aragon "Ferdinand II of Aragon") and [Queen Isabella I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_I_of_Castile "Isabella I of Castile") from the [Emirate of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Granada "Emirate of Granada"), which completed the _[reconquista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista "Reconquista")_. During the colonial era, Granada was a [sister city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sister_city "Sister city") to the settlement of [Antigua Guatemala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antigua_Guatemala "Antigua Guatemala"), maintained a flourishing level of commerce with ports in the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") via [Lake Cocibolca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua") and the [San Juan River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juan_River_(Nicaragua) "San Juan River (Nicaragua)"), and was subject to attacks from [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_people "English people"), [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people "French people") and [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_people "Dutch people")[pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piracy_in_the_Caribbean "Piracy in the Caribbean") who unsuccessfully attempted to take control of the settlement by sailing up the San Juan River.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-3)

For many years Granada disputed with [León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n,_Nicaragua "León, Nicaragua") its hegemony as the major city of Nicaragua. The city of Granada was favored by the [Conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism "Conservatism"), while Léon was favored by the [Liberals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism "Liberalism"). For many years there was conflict that at times became quite violent between the cities' families and political factions. In the mid-19th century a compromise site was agreed on and the capital was finally established at [Managua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managua "Managua") between both cities.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] As of 1850, Granada had a population of approximately 10,000.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-Baily-4)

On 29 May 1834, [Cándido Flores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A1ndido_Flores?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cándido Flores (page does not exist)"), head of the military forces of Granada, revolted against the Government in [León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n,_Nicaragua "León, Nicaragua") led by [José Núñez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_N%C3%BA%C3%B1ez_(President_of_Nicaragua) "José Núñez (President of Nicaragua)"), demanding the reform of the federal Constitution. After being defeated in Managua he could not organize a resistance in Granada, so he left the city to a disorganized mob that committed lootings and robberies, especially in the houses of foreigners.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-5)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/General_Walker_Reviewing_Troops_on_the_Grand_Plaza%2C_Granada%2C_Capital_of_Nicaragua_-_FL_1856.jpg/250px-General_Walker_Reviewing_Troops_on_the_Grand_Plaza%2C_Granada%2C_Capital_of_Nicaragua_-_FL_1856.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:General_Walker_Reviewing_Troops_on_the_Grand_Plaza,_Granada,_Capital_of_Nicaragua_-_FL_1856.jpg)

American-born General William [Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Walker_(filibuster) "William Walker (filibuster)") reviewing his troops on the Grand Plaza, Granada, capital of Nicaragua. Illustration for Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper, June 21 of 1856.

Granada was also the site where American [filibuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filibuster_(military) "Filibuster (military)")[William Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Walker_(filibuster) "William Walker (filibuster)") took up residence and attempted to take control of [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America") and create independent colonies with economies based on slavery. One of Walker's generals, [Charles Frederick Henningsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Frederick_Henningsen "Charles Frederick Henningsen"), set the city ablaze before escaping, destroying much of the colonial-era architecture and inscribed the words "Here was Granada" on the ruins before he left.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-7)

Granada avoided much of the tumult of the [Sandinista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandinista "Sandinista") Era in the 1970–80s.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/St_Francis_Church_Granada_Nicaragua.jpg/250px-St_Francis_Church_Granada_Nicaragua.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_Francis_Church_Granada_Nicaragua.jpg)

San Francisco Convent Church, built in 1685-late 18th century by the [Franciscans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franciscans "Franciscans").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-10)

Granada is located along the coast of the [Lake Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua") (a.k.a. Lake Cocibolca), the world's twentieth largest lake.

Physiographically, the city occupies a low-lying alluvial terrace within the Nicaraguan Depression (or Central Nicaraguan Graben), bounded by the volcanic flanks of [Mombacho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombacho "Mombacho") to the south and the tectonic basin of [Lake Cocibolca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua") to the east.

Granada is the capital city of the Department of Granada, which borders Boaco and [Managua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managua "Managua") to the north, Masaya and Carazo to the east and Rivas to the south. Within the same department, the River Tipitapa which connects the Lake of Managua and Nicaragua passes through it in the north. It also has three volcanic lagoons; Manares, Genirzaro, and the famous Apoyo. Apoyo, which is shared with the Department of Masaya, is the largest volcanic lagoon in Nicaragua.

Granada is a very warm city all year round, with very similar temperatures to Managua. This is due to similarities in geography with its close proximity to a lake and surrounded by high hills. Rainfall in Granada is approximately between 1,100 and 2,100 mm annually, with an annual average temperature reported to be 25.7°C. [[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-11)

The vegetation around Granada is a reflection of its climatology. Dry and humid forests skirt the [Mombacho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombacho "Mombacho") volcano. The volcano is also home to a wide array of [fauna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna "Fauna")_(See [Wildlife of Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildlife\_of\_Nicaragua "Wildlife of Nicaragua"))_. The lake is also home to many creatures, both marine and freshwater creatures. It is the only freshwater lake in the world where sharks live ([Nicaragua shark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua_shark "Nicaragua shark")). Fishing in the lake is quite good, and fishermen, both commercial and recreational, regularly catch [guapote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parachromis "Parachromis") and [mojarras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mojarra "Mojarra"), as well as [sardines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardine "Sardine"). Nicaragua has recently banned fishing of the Nicaragua shark and [sawfish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sawfish "Sawfish") because of population decline.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-12)

Other cities and towns within the Granada district include Malacatoya, El Paso, El Guayabo, Diria, Macatepe, El Guanacaste, [Nandaime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandaime "Nandaime") and Diriomo, known nationally as the last city of witches. Mombacho volcano is the highest point (1,345 m) within Granada; the now dormant volcano blew most of its cone into the lake, forming the 365 [Islets of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islets_of_Granada "Islets of Granada"). It is also possible on a clear day to see [Ometepe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ometepe "Ometepe") and [Zapatera Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zapatera_Island "Zapatera Island").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The later island is the second largest island in [Lake Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua"), and also harbors an inactive volcano. The largest is Ometepe Island, also located in Lake Nicaragua. Several [pre-Columbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian "Pre-Columbian") statues and idols were found on the island during the [Spanish conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest "Spanish conquest"), and now exhibited in the Convento San Francisco Museum, as well as in other museums and parks located on Ometepe Island.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-13)

Granada has several beaches on Lake Nicaragua which are very popular around [Semana Santa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semana_Santa "Semana Santa") ("Holy Week").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
