[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Granada%2C_Nicaragua_4.jpg/250px-Granada%2C_Nicaragua_4.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Granada,_Nicaragua_4.jpg)

Xalteva Church, it was originally built during colonial times and due to its location it was used as a military fortress. The façade and interior were rebuilt after its destruction by [William Walker the filibuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Walker_(filibuster) "William Walker (filibuster)"), it was finally rebuilt in 1890–1898.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-18)

Granada has long been a center of commerce, including [timber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timber "Timber"), [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold "Gold") and [silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver "Silver"). Granada's economy continues to grow as it is becoming a hub for tourism. Though Granada remains Nicaragua's sixth largest city, it is widely known for preserving some of the finest colonial-era architecture in the country.

A real estate boom had been underway for several years, with many European and Americans purchasing and renovating the area's homes for retirement or holiday homes and several foreign realtors establishing offices, but that boom slowed in 2007. The prior escalation of real estate prices in Granada and other parts of Southwestern Nicaragua has led to a shift of investor attention toward Northern Nicaragua and the cities of [Matagalpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matagalpa "Matagalpa"), Leon, [Corinto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corinto,_Nicaragua "Corinto, Nicaragua") and the surrounding beaches of Leon and Corinto.

Museums have opened, and new hotels and restaurants are proliferating at a fast rate.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Granada, though now dependent on tourism, also has fertile agricultural land within the municipality. Major production of organic [coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee "Coffee") and [cacao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocoa_bean "Cocoa bean"), [cattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cattle "Cattle"), [plantains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plantain_(cooking) "Plantain (cooking)") and [bananas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banana "Banana") occurs within its boundaries.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Gastronomy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Gastronomy")]

See also: [Tourism in Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Nicaragua "Tourism in Nicaragua")

Granada's restaurants have received recognition by newspapers like the New York Times.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-19) In the city of Granada, there are a number of restaurants including Pita Pita, Garden Café & La Hacienda. In recent years,[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] the city of Granada's evolving culinary scene mixes local and international flavors, as well as supporting [farm-to-table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farm-to-table "Farm-to-table") sustainability of local growers and producers.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Granada's economy continues to grow in big part because it has become a tourist attraction for its colonial architecture, as well as its ecology and now as a food destination.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-20)

## Infrastructure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Infrastructure")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Typical_Nicaraguan_street.JPG/250px-Typical_Nicaraguan_street.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Typical_Nicaraguan_street.JPG)

A street of Granada

Most of Granada's streets are narrow, as the city evolved centuries before the advent of motorized vehicles. Therefore, today, many streets allow only one-way traffic, offering a challenge to visitors traveling by car.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Following many years of neglect, primarily due to the economic collapse of the nation in the 1980s, most of Granada's buildings and [infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure "Infrastructure") began to deteriorate. Roads and public utilities fell into disrepair.

In the decades that followed, however, the city government directed funds towards recognition and [restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_restoration "Building restoration") of many of Granada's historic structures. The Spanish government has provided financial cooperation for the refurbishment of the city. One such project is transforming Calle La Calzada into a pedestrian street.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-21)

## Culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Culture")]

See also: [Culture of Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_Nicaragua "Culture of Nicaragua")

Granada, like most of the Nicaraguan Pacific, is populated primarily by a Spanish-speaking majority of [Mestizos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo"). Residing here also are people from the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland"), [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria"), the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), and [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France").

Until recently, Nicaragua was experiencing a booming tourist economy. This, in turn, attracted foreigners to Granada seeking colonial homes for purchase, adding a growing number of Europeans and Americans to the city's population. Real estate prices had increased following the foreign interest and subsequent investments. However, with the 2018 civil conflict, the US Department of State issued a travel advisory, citing "civil unrest, crime, limited healthcare availability, and arbitrary enforcement of laws."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-22) In 2020, it issued a Level 4, "Do Not Travel" advisory due to COVID-19.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua#cite_note-23) The city is recognized as a "[Design City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_Cities_(UNESCO) "Design Cities (UNESCO)")" by [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")'s [Creative Cities Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Cities_Network "Creative Cities Network").

With an estimated population of 105,862 (2022),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit#) it is Nicaragua's ninth most populous city. Granada is historically one of Nicaragua's most important cities, economically and politically. It has a rich colonial heritage, seen in its architecture and structure. Granada had a thriving indigenous population. In 1524, the city was renamed Granada, by !Image 24![Image 25Francisco Hernández de Córdoba!Image 26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Hern%C3%A1ndez_de_C%C3%B3rdoba_(founder_of_Nicaragua) "Francisco Hernández de Córdoba (founder of Nicaragua)")!Image 27, ostensibly the first European city in mainland America. Unlike other cities that claim the same distinction, the city of Granada was not only the settlement of the conquest, but also a city registered in official records of the Crown of Aragon, and the Kingdom of Castile in Spain. With an estimated population of 105,862 (2022),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit#) it is Nicaragua's ninth most populous city. Granada is historically one of Nicaragua's most important cities, economically and politically. It has a rich colonial heritage, seen in its architecture and structure. Granada had a thriving indigenous population. In 1524, the city was renamed Granada, by !Image 24![Image 25Francisco Hernández de Córdoba!Image 26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Hern%C3%A1ndez_de_C%C3%B3rdoba_(founder_of_Nicaragua) "Francisco Hernández de Córdoba (founder of Nicaragua)")!Image 27, ostensibly the first European city in mainland America. Unlike other cities that claim the same distinction, the city of Granada was not only the settlement of the conquest, but also a city registered in official records of the Crown of Aragon, and the Kingdom of Castile in Spain. Granada is the capital city of the Department of Granada, which borders Boaco and !Image 179![Image 180Managua!Image 181](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managua "Managua")!Image 182 to the north, Masaya and Carazo to the east and Rivas to the south. Within the same department, the River Tipitapa which connects the Lake of Managua and Nicaragua passes through it in the north. It also has three volcanic lagoons; Manares, Genirzaro, and the famous Apoyo. Apoyo, which is shared with the Department of Masaya, is the largest volcanic lagoon in Nicaragua. Granada is a very warm city all year round, with very similar temperatures to Managua. This is due to similarities in geography with its close proximity to a lake and surrounded by high hills. Rainfall in Granada is approximately between 1,100 and 2,100 mm annually, with an annual average temperature reported to be 25.7°C.↵[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit#)!Image 183 The vegetation around Granada is a reflection of its climatology. **Granada** (Spanish pronunciation:[[ɡɾaˈnaða]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) is a city in western [Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua "Nicaragua") and the capital of the [Granada Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_Department "Granada Department"). With an estimated population of 105,862 (2022),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-2) it is Nicaragua's ninth most populous city. Granada is historically one of Nicaragua's most important cities, economically and politically. It has a rich colonial heritage, seen in its architecture and structure.

Granada had a thriving indigenous population. In 1524, the city was renamed Granada, by [Francisco Hernández de Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Hern%C3%A1ndez_de_C%C3%B3rdoba_(founder_of_Nicaragua) "Francisco Hernández de Córdoba (founder of Nicaragua)"), ostensibly the first European city in mainland America. Unlike other cities that claim the same distinction, the city of Granada was not only the settlement of the conquest, but also a city registered in official records of the Crown of Aragon, and the Kingdom of Castile in Spain.

Granada is also known as _La Gran Sultana_, in the reflection of its Moorish and Andalusian appearance, unlike its sister city and historical rival [León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n_(Nicaragua) "León (Nicaragua)"), which displays Castilian trends.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/GranadaNicaragua1900.jpg/250px-GranadaNicaragua1900.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GranadaNicaragua1900.jpg)

Granada street scene, circa 1905

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Old_Market_Building_of_Granada%2C_Nicaragua_in_1880.jpg/250px-Old_Market_Building_of_Granada%2C_Nicaragua_in_1880.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Old_Market_Building_of_Granada,_Nicaragua_in_1880.jpg)

Old Market Building of Granada in 1880

The settlement of Granada was established by Spanish conquistador [Hernández de Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Hern%C3%A1ndez_de_C%C3%B3rdoba_(founder_of_Nicaragua) "Francisco Hernández de Córdoba (founder of Nicaragua)"), who named it after the city of the same name in Spain. This was done in honor of [the city's capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_War "Granada War") by the forces of [King Ferdinand II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_Aragon "Ferdinand II of Aragon") and [Queen Isabella I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_I_of_Castile "Isabella I of Castile") from the [Emirate of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Granada "Emirate of Granada"), which completed the _[reconquista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista "Reconquista")_. During the colonial era, Granada was a [sister city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sister_city "Sister city") to the settlement of [Antigua Guatemala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antigua_Guatemala "Antigua Guatemala"), maintained a flourishing level of commerce with ports in the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") via [Lake Cocibolca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua") and the [San Juan River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juan_River_(Nicaragua) "San Juan River (Nicaragua)"), and was subject to attacks from [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_people "English people"), [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people "French people") and [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_people "Dutch people")[pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piracy_in_the_Caribbean "Piracy in the Caribbean") who unsuccessfully attempted to take control of the settlement by sailing up the San Juan River.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-3)

For many years Granada disputed with [León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n,_Nicaragua "León, Nicaragua") its hegemony as the major city of Nicaragua. The city of Granada was favored by the [Conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism "Conservatism"), while Léon was favored by the [Liberals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism "Liberalism"). For many years there was conflict that at times became quite violent between the cities' families and political factions. In the mid-19th century a compromise site was agreed on and the capital was finally established at [Managua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managua "Managua") between both cities.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] As of 1850, Granada had a population of approximately 10,000.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-Baily-4)

On 29 May 1834, [Cándido Flores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A1ndido_Flores?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cándido Flores (page does not exist)"), head of the military forces of Granada, revolted against the Government in [León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n,_Nicaragua "León, Nicaragua") led by [José Núñez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_N%C3%BA%C3%B1ez_(President_of_Nicaragua) "José Núñez (President of Nicaragua)"), demanding the reform of the federal Constitution. After being defeated in Managua he could not organize a resistance in Granada, so he left the city to a disorganized mob that committed lootings and robberies, especially in the houses of foreigners.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-5)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/General_Walker_Reviewing_Troops_on_the_Grand_Plaza%2C_Granada%2C_Capital_of_Nicaragua_-_FL_1856.jpg/250px-General_Walker_Reviewing_Troops_on_the_Grand_Plaza%2C_Granada%2C_Capital_of_Nicaragua_-_FL_1856.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:General_Walker_Reviewing_Troops_on_the_Grand_Plaza,_Granada,_Capital_of_Nicaragua_-_FL_1856.jpg)

American-born General William [Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Walker_(filibuster) "William Walker (filibuster)") reviewing his troops on the Grand Plaza, Granada, capital of Nicaragua. Illustration for Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper, June 21 of 1856.

Granada was also the site where American [filibuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filibuster_(military) "Filibuster (military)")[William Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Walker_(filibuster) "William Walker (filibuster)") took up residence and attempted to take control of [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America") and create independent colonies with economies based on slavery. One of Walker's generals, [Charles Frederick Henningsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Frederick_Henningsen "Charles Frederick Henningsen"), set the city ablaze before escaping, destroying much of the colonial-era architecture and inscribed the words "Here was Granada" on the ruins before he left.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-7)

Granada avoided much of the tumult of the [Sandinista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandinista "Sandinista") Era in the 1970–80s.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/St_Francis_Church_Granada_Nicaragua.jpg/250px-St_Francis_Church_Granada_Nicaragua.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_Francis_Church_Granada_Nicaragua.jpg)

San Francisco Convent Church, built in 1685-late 18th century by the [Franciscans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franciscans "Franciscans").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-10)

Granada is located along the coast of the [Lake Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua") (a.k.a. Lake Cocibolca), the world's twentieth largest lake.

Physiographically, the city occupies a low-lying alluvial terrace within the Nicaraguan Depression (or Central Nicaraguan Graben), bounded by the volcanic flanks of [Mombacho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombacho "Mombacho") to the south and the tectonic basin of [Lake Cocibolca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua") to the east.

Granada is the capital city of the Department of Granada, which borders Boaco and [Managua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managua "Managua") to the north, Masaya and Carazo to the east and Rivas to the south. Within the same department, the River Tipitapa which connects the Lake of Managua and Nicaragua passes through it in the north. It also has three volcanic lagoons; Manares, Genirzaro, and the famous Apoyo. Apoyo, which is shared with the Department of Masaya, is the largest volcanic lagoon in Nicaragua.

Granada is a very warm city all year round, with very similar temperatures to Managua. This is due to similarities in geography with its close proximity to a lake and surrounded by high hills. Rainfall in Granada is approximately between 1,100 and 2,100 mm annually, with an annual average temperature reported to be 25.7°C. [[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-11)

The vegetation around Granada is a reflection of its climatology. Dry and humid forests skirt the [Mombacho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombacho "Mombacho") volcano. The volcano is also home to a wide array of [fauna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna "Fauna")_(See [Wildlife of Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildlife\_of\_Nicaragua "Wildlife of Nicaragua"))_. The lake is also home to many creatures, both marine and freshwater creatures. It is the only freshwater lake in the world where sharks live ([Nicaragua shark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua_shark "Nicaragua shark")). Fishing in the lake is quite good, and fishermen, both commercial and recreational, regularly catch [guapote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parachromis "Parachromis") and [mojarras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mojarra "Mojarra"), as well as [sardines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardine "Sardine"). Nicaragua has recently banned fishing of the Nicaragua shark and [sawfish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sawfish "Sawfish") because of population decline.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-12)

Other cities and towns within the Granada district include Malacatoya, El Paso, El Guayabo, Diria, Macatepe, El Guanacaste, [Nandaime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandaime "Nandaime") and Diriomo, known nationally as the last city of witches. Mombacho volcano is the highest point (1,345 m) within Granada; the now dormant volcano blew most of its cone into the lake, forming the 365 [Islets of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islets_of_Granada "Islets of Granada"). It is also possible on a clear day to see [Ometepe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ometepe "Ometepe") and [Zapatera Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zapatera_Island "Zapatera Island").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The later island is the second largest island in [Lake Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua"), and also harbors an inactive volcano. The largest is Ometepe Island, also located in Lake Nicaragua. Several [pre-Columbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian "Pre-Columbian") statues and idols were found on the island during the [Spanish conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest "Spanish conquest"), and now exhibited in the Convento San Francisco Museum, as well as in other museums and parks located on Ometepe Island.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-13)

Granada has several beaches on Lake Nicaragua which are very popular around [Semana Santa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semana_Santa "Semana Santa") ("Holy Week").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Economy and tourism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Economy and tourism")]

See also: [Tourism in Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Nicaragua "Tourism in Nicaragua")

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Calle_Atravesada.jpg/250px-Calle_Atravesada.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Calle_Atravesada.jpg)

Atravesada street

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/La_Merced_Church-Granada%2C_Nicaragua.jpg/250px-La_Merced_Church-Granada%2C_Nicaragua.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:La_Merced_Church-Granada,_Nicaragua.jpg)

Preserved Colonial Church of Nuestra Señora de la Merced, built in 1534–1783, by the [Order of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mercy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Blessed_Virgin_Mary_of_Mercy "Order of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mercy").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-15)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Catedral_de_Granada%2C_Nicaragua.jpg/250px-Catedral_de_Granada%2C_Nicaragua.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Catedral_de_Granada,_Nicaragua.jpg)

[Granada Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Our_Lady_of_the_Assumption_Cathedral,_Granada "Our Lady of the Assumption Cathedral, Granada") built in 1751.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-16)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Granada%2C_Nicaragua_4.jpg/250px-Granada%2C_Nicaragua_4.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Granada,_Nicaragua_4.jpg)

Xalteva Church, it was originally built during colonial times and due to its location it was used as a military fortress. The façade and interior were rebuilt after its destruction by [William Walker the filibuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Walker_(filibuster) "William Walker (filibuster)"), it was finally rebuilt in 1890–1898.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-18)

Granada has long been a center of commerce, including [timber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timber "Timber"), [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold "Gold") and [silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver "Silver"). Granada's economy continues to grow as it is becoming a hub for tourism. Though Granada remains Nicaragua's sixth largest city, it is widely known for preserving some of the finest colonial-era architecture in the country.

A real estate boom had been underway for several years, with many European and Americans purchasing and renovating the area's homes for retirement or holiday homes and several foreign realtors establishing offices, but that boom slowed in 2007. The prior escalation of real estate prices in Granada and other parts of Southwestern Nicaragua has led to a shift of investor attention toward Northern Nicaragua and the cities of [Matagalpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matagalpa "Matagalpa"), Leon, [Corinto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corinto,_Nicaragua "Corinto, Nicaragua") and the surrounding beaches of Leon and Corinto.

Museums have opened, and new hotels and restaurants are proliferating at a fast rate.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Granada, though now dependent on tourism, also has fertile agricultural land within the municipality. Major production of organic [coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee "Coffee") and [cacao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocoa_bean "Cocoa bean"), [cattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cattle "Cattle"), [plantains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plantain_(cooking) "Plantain (cooking)") and [bananas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banana "Banana") occurs within its boundaries.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Gastronomy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Gastronomy")]

See also: [Tourism in Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Nicaragua "Tourism in Nicaragua")

Granada's restaurants have received recognition by newspapers like the New York Times.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-19) In the city of Granada, there are a number of restaurants including Pita Pita, Garden Café & La Hacienda. In recent years,[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] the city of Granada's evolving culinary scene mixes local and international flavors, as well as supporting [farm-to-table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farm-to-table "Farm-to-table") sustainability of local growers and producers.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Granada's economy continues to grow in big part because it has become a tourist attraction for its colonial architecture, as well as its ecology and now as a food destination.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-20)

## Infrastructure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Infrastructure")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Typical_Nicaraguan_street.JPG/250px-Typical_Nicaraguan_street.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Typical_Nicaraguan_street.JPG)

A street of Granada

Most of Granada's streets are narrow, as the city evolved centuries before the advent of motorized vehicles. Therefore, today, many streets allow only one-way traffic, offering a challenge to visitors traveling by car.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Following many years of neglect, primarily due to the economic collapse of the nation in the 1980s, most of Granada's buildings and [infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure "Infrastructure") began to deteriorate. Roads and public utilities fell into disrepair.

In the decades that followed, however, the city government directed funds towards recognition and [restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_restoration "Building restoration") of many of Granada's historic structures. The Spanish government has provided financial cooperation for the refurbishment of the city. One such project is transforming Calle La Calzada into a pedestrian street.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-21)

## Culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Culture")]

See also: [Culture of Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_Nicaragua "Culture of Nicaragua")

Granada, like most of the Nicaraguan Pacific, is populated primarily by a Spanish-speaking majority of [Mestizos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo"). Residing here also are people from the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland"), [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria"), the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), and [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France").

Until recently, Nicaragua was experiencing a booming tourist economy. This, in turn, attracted foreigners to Granada seeking colonial homes for purchase, adding a growing number of Europeans and Americans to the city's population. Real estate prices had increased following the foreign interest and subsequent investments. However, with the 2018 civil conflict, the US Department of State issued a travel advisory, citing "civil unrest, crime, limited healthcare availability, and arbitrary enforcement of laws."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-22) In 2020, it issued a Level 4, "Do Not Travel" advisory due to COVID-19.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-23) The city is recognized as a "[Design City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_Cities_(UNESCO) "Design Cities (UNESCO)")" by [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")'s [Creative Cities Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Cities_Network "Creative Cities Network").

**Granada** (Spanish pronunciation:[[ɡɾaˈnaða]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) is a city in western [Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua "Nicaragua") and the capital of the [Granada Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_Department "Granada Department"). With an estimated population of 105,862 (2022),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-2) it is Nicaragua's ninth most populous city. Granada is historically one of Nicaragua's most important cities, economically and politically. It has a rich colonial heritage, seen in its architecture and structure.

Granada had a thriving indigenous population. In 1524, the city was renamed Granada, by [Francisco Hernández de Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Hern%C3%A1ndez_de_C%C3%B3rdoba_(founder_of_Nicaragua) "Francisco Hernández de Córdoba (founder of Nicaragua)"), ostensibly the first European city in mainland America. Unlike other cities that claim the same distinction, the city of Granada was not only the settlement of the conquest, but also a city registered in official records of the Crown of Aragon, and the Kingdom of Castile in Spain.

Granada is also known as _La Gran Sultana_, in the reflection of its Moorish and Andalusian appearance, unlike its sister city and historical rival [León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n_(Nicaragua) "León (Nicaragua)"), which displays Castilian trends.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/GranadaNicaragua1900.jpg/250px-GranadaNicaragua1900.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GranadaNicaragua1900.jpg)

Granada street scene, circa 1905

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Old_Market_Building_of_Granada%2C_Nicaragua_in_1880.jpg/250px-Old_Market_Building_of_Granada%2C_Nicaragua_in_1880.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Old_Market_Building_of_Granada,_Nicaragua_in_1880.jpg)

Old Market Building of Granada in 1880

The settlement of Granada was established by Spanish conquistador [Hernández de Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Hern%C3%A1ndez_de_C%C3%B3rdoba_(founder_of_Nicaragua) "Francisco Hernández de Córdoba (founder of Nicaragua)"), who named it after the city of the same name in Spain. This was done in honor of [the city's capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_War "Granada War") by the forces of [King Ferdinand II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_Aragon "Ferdinand II of Aragon") and [Queen Isabella I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_I_of_Castile "Isabella I of Castile") from the [Emirate of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Granada "Emirate of Granada"), which completed the _[reconquista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista "Reconquista")_. During the colonial era, Granada was a [sister city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sister_city "Sister city") to the settlement of [Antigua Guatemala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antigua_Guatemala "Antigua Guatemala"), maintained a flourishing level of commerce with ports in the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") via [Lake Cocibolca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua") and the [San Juan River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juan_River_(Nicaragua) "San Juan River (Nicaragua)"), and was subject to attacks from [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_people "English people"), [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people "French people") and [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_people "Dutch people")[pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piracy_in_the_Caribbean "Piracy in the Caribbean") who unsuccessfully attempted to take control of the settlement by sailing up the San Juan River.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-3)

For many years Granada disputed with [León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n,_Nicaragua "León, Nicaragua") its hegemony as the major city of Nicaragua. The city of Granada was favored by the [Conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism "Conservatism"), while Léon was favored by the [Liberals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism "Liberalism"). For many years there was conflict that at times became quite violent between the cities' families and political factions. In the mid-19th century a compromise site was agreed on and the capital was finally established at [Managua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managua "Managua") between both cities.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] As of 1850, Granada had a population of approximately 10,000.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-Baily-4)

On 29 May 1834, [Cándido Flores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A1ndido_Flores?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cándido Flores (page does not exist)"), head of the military forces of Granada, revolted against the Government in [León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n,_Nicaragua "León, Nicaragua") led by [José Núñez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_N%C3%BA%C3%B1ez_(President_of_Nicaragua) "José Núñez (President of Nicaragua)"), demanding the reform of the federal Constitution. After being defeated in Managua he could not organize a resistance in Granada, so he left the city to a disorganized mob that committed lootings and robberies, especially in the houses of foreigners.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-5)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/General_Walker_Reviewing_Troops_on_the_Grand_Plaza%2C_Granada%2C_Capital_of_Nicaragua_-_FL_1856.jpg/250px-General_Walker_Reviewing_Troops_on_the_Grand_Plaza%2C_Granada%2C_Capital_of_Nicaragua_-_FL_1856.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:General_Walker_Reviewing_Troops_on_the_Grand_Plaza,_Granada,_Capital_of_Nicaragua_-_FL_1856.jpg)

American-born General William [Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Walker_(filibuster) "William Walker (filibuster)") reviewing his troops on the Grand Plaza, Granada, capital of Nicaragua. Illustration for Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper, June 21 of 1856.

Granada was also the site where American [filibuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filibuster_(military) "Filibuster (military)")[William Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Walker_(filibuster) "William Walker (filibuster)") took up residence and attempted to take control of [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America") and create independent colonies with economies based on slavery. One of Walker's generals, [Charles Frederick Henningsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Frederick_Henningsen "Charles Frederick Henningsen"), set the city ablaze before escaping, destroying much of the colonial-era architecture and inscribed the words "Here was Granada" on the ruins before he left.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-7)

Granada avoided much of the tumult of the [Sandinista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandinista "Sandinista") Era in the 1970–80s.

San Francisco Convent Church, built in 1685-late 18th century by the [Franciscans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franciscans "Franciscans").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-10)

Granada is located along the coast of the [Lake Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua") (a.k.a. Lake Cocibolca), the world's twentieth largest lake.

Physiographically, the city occupies a low-lying alluvial terrace within the Nicaraguan Depression (or Central Nicaraguan Graben), bounded by the volcanic flanks of [Mombacho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombacho "Mombacho") to the south and the tectonic basin of [Lake Cocibolca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua") to the east.

Granada is the capital city of the Department of Granada, which borders Boaco and [Managua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managua "Managua") to the north, Masaya and Carazo to the east and Rivas to the south. Within the same department, the River Tipitapa which connects the Lake of Managua and Nicaragua passes through it in the north. It also has three volcanic lagoons; Manares, Genirzaro, and the famous Apoyo. Apoyo, which is shared with the Department of Masaya, is the largest volcanic lagoon in Nicaragua.

Granada is a very warm city all year round, with very similar temperatures to Managua. This is due to similarities in geography with its close proximity to a lake and surrounded by high hills. Rainfall in Granada is approximately between 1,100 and 2,100 mm annually, with an annual average temperature reported to be 25.7°C. [[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-11)

The vegetation around Granada is a reflection of its climatology. Dry and humid forests skirt the [Mombacho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombacho "Mombacho") volcano. The volcano is also home to a wide array of [fauna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna "Fauna")_(See [Wildlife of Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildlife\_of\_Nicaragua "Wildlife of Nicaragua"))_. The lake is also home to many creatures, both marine and freshwater creatures. It is the only freshwater lake in the world where sharks live ([Nicaragua shark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua_shark "Nicaragua shark")). Fishing in the lake is quite good, and fishermen, both commercial and recreational, regularly catch [guapote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parachromis "Parachromis") and [mojarras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mojarra "Mojarra"), as well as [sardines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardine "Sardine"). Nicaragua has recently banned fishing of the Nicaragua shark and [sawfish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sawfish "Sawfish") because of population decline.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-12)

Other cities and towns within the Granada district include Malacatoya, El Paso, El Guayabo, Diria, Macatepe, El Guanacaste, [Nandaime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandaime "Nandaime") and Diriomo, known nationally as the last city of witches. Mombacho volcano is the highest point (1,345 m) within Granada; the now dormant volcano blew most of its cone into the lake, forming the 365 [Islets of Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islets_of_Granada "Islets of Granada"). It is also possible on a clear day to see [Ometepe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ometepe "Ometepe") and [Zapatera Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zapatera_Island "Zapatera Island").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The later island is the second largest island in [Lake Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua"), and also harbors an inactive volcano. The largest is Ometepe Island, also located in Lake Nicaragua. Several [pre-Columbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian "Pre-Columbian") statues and idols were found on the island during the [Spanish conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest "Spanish conquest"), and now exhibited in the Convento San Francisco Museum, as well as in other museums and parks located on Ometepe Island.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-13)

Granada has several beaches on Lake Nicaragua which are very popular around [Semana Santa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semana_Santa "Semana Santa") ("Holy Week").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Granada%2C_Nicaragua_4.jpg/250px-Granada%2C_Nicaragua_4.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Granada,_Nicaragua_4.jpg)

Xalteva Church, it was originally built during colonial times and due to its location it was used as a military fortress. The façade and interior were rebuilt after its destruction by [William Walker the filibuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Walker_(filibuster) "William Walker (filibuster)"), it was finally rebuilt in 1890–1898.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-18)

Granada has long been a center of commerce, including [timber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timber "Timber"), [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold "Gold") and [silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver "Silver"). Granada's economy continues to grow as it is becoming a hub for tourism. Though Granada remains Nicaragua's sixth largest city, it is widely known for preserving some of the finest colonial-era architecture in the country.

A real estate boom had been underway for several years, with many European and Americans purchasing and renovating the area's homes for retirement or holiday homes and several foreign realtors establishing offices, but that boom slowed in 2007. The prior escalation of real estate prices in Granada and other parts of Southwestern Nicaragua has led to a shift of investor attention toward Northern Nicaragua and the cities of [Matagalpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matagalpa "Matagalpa"), Leon, [Corinto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corinto,_Nicaragua "Corinto, Nicaragua") and the surrounding beaches of Leon and Corinto.

Museums have opened, and new hotels and restaurants are proliferating at a fast rate.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Granada, though now dependent on tourism, also has fertile agricultural land within the municipality. Major production of organic [coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee "Coffee") and [cacao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocoa_bean "Cocoa bean"), [cattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cattle "Cattle"), [plantains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plantain_(cooking) "Plantain (cooking)") and [bananas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banana "Banana") occurs within its boundaries.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Gastronomy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Gastronomy")]

See also: [Tourism in Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Nicaragua "Tourism in Nicaragua")

Granada's restaurants have received recognition by newspapers like the New York Times.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-19) In the city of Granada, there are a number of restaurants including Pita Pita, Garden Café & La Hacienda. In recent years,[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] the city of Granada's evolving culinary scene mixes local and international flavors, as well as supporting [farm-to-table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farm-to-table "Farm-to-table") sustainability of local growers and producers.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Granada's economy continues to grow in big part because it has become a tourist attraction for its colonial architecture, as well as its ecology and now as a food destination.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-20)

## Infrastructure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Infrastructure")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Typical_Nicaraguan_street.JPG/250px-Typical_Nicaraguan_street.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Typical_Nicaraguan_street.JPG)

A street of Granada

Most of Granada's streets are narrow, as the city evolved centuries before the advent of motorized vehicles. Therefore, today, many streets allow only one-way traffic, offering a challenge to visitors traveling by car.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Following many years of neglect, primarily due to the economic collapse of the nation in the 1980s, most of Granada's buildings and [infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure "Infrastructure") began to deteriorate. Roads and public utilities fell into disrepair.

In the decades that followed, however, the city government directed funds towards recognition and [restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_restoration "Building restoration") of many of Granada's historic structures. The Spanish government has provided financial cooperation for the refurbishment of the city. One such project is transforming Calle La Calzada into a pedestrian street.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-21)

## Culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Culture")]

See also: [Culture of Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_Nicaragua "Culture of Nicaragua")

Granada, like most of the Nicaraguan Pacific, is populated primarily by a Spanish-speaking majority of [Mestizos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo"). Residing here also are people from the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland"), [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria"), the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), and [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France").

Until recently, Nicaragua was experiencing a booming tourist economy. This, in turn, attracted foreigners to Granada seeking colonial homes for purchase, adding a growing number of Europeans and Americans to the city's population. Real estate prices had increased following the foreign interest and subsequent investments. However, with the 2018 civil conflict, the US Department of State issued a travel advisory, citing "civil unrest, crime, limited healthcare availability, and arbitrary enforcement of laws."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-22) In 2020, it issued a Level 4, "Do Not Travel" advisory due to COVID-19.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Granada,_Nicaragua&search=fountain#cite_note-23) The city is recognized as a "[Design City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_Cities_(UNESCO) "Design Cities (UNESCO)")" by [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")'s [Creative Cities Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Cities_Network "Creative Cities Network").
